Add decant-trace crate with Perfetto JSON tracing, optional Tracy and summary CLI

Thread local spans, lock waits, counters and frame marks are recorded when
DECANT_TRACE is set and written as Chrome and Perfetto JSON by flush and at
process exit. With the variable unset or 0 every call is one relaxed load of
an AtomicBool and allocates nothing. The optional tracy feature forwards
spans, plots and frame marks to tracy-client. decant_trace_summary prints
the top spans by total and max time, per thread active time and the lock
wait hotspots of a trace.

Closes #17

an_untouched_page_is_a_reserved_mapped_page_until_its_first_access_through_any_view
failed on machines that grant the lock memory privilege. A 64 page pool (4 MiB)
is a multiple of the 2 MiB large page granule, so section() took
SEC_COMMIT | SEC_LARGE_PAGES and the page was committed at map time
(VirtualQuery gave MEM_COMMIT right after map_frames). The test now loads 65
pages, which gives normal pages and SEC_RESERVE, and is skipped under Wine,
which commits the whole section too. The engine is unchanged.

Stand in for the title's upscaler with a pass of ours

As Series S the title renders 1280x720 and has AMD's upscaler make the
1920x1080 picture. Its passes are console-compiled programs the translator
does not read, so the output stayed black (ss_try4). The runtime now hands
the title's lookup of the upscaler's ffxDispatch a function of ours: an
upscale dispatch becomes one pass that draws the colour input over the
output with linear filtering, after which the title's state is set again
on the list. Other dispatches go to the upscaler as before.
VICTORY_UPSCALE=title leaves the upscaler alone.

ss_up1 (Series S): the opening cutscene shows, 88-146 ms a frame (286-420
as Series X in batch_try1), no device errors. Faces are lit. Hair is
missing and the picture is softer than the upscaler's would be.

feat: GPU: scattered indirect records clamped once per list (VICTORY_INDIRECT_GATHER=1)

A single indirect record that misses its window gets a slot that the list's
prelude fills in one clamp pass by a table of offsets, instead of a compute
pass of ours in front of its draw. Gathering ends at a dispatch or at a draw
whose shaders can store to buffers. Off by default; needs
VICTORY_INDIRECT_WINDOW=1. Manual port: our clamp shader uses bit 3 of
has_count for gathered records (bit 2 is our dispatch split), and the
diagnostics counters, window check and card meter of the source are left out.

feat: GPU: fresh staging buffer instead of settling for one in flight (VICTORY_STAGING_DOUBLE=1)

A texture whose staging buffer a list or a flight still holds was
recorded into again, so the submission settled (waited for the card)
for it: about 12 settles and 60 ms a frame in the world. With the switch
a fresh buffer takes the texture's place for the list recording it; the
old one lives on with its holders. Reuse needs no holder besides the map
and no unfinished submission on the buffer (texture::reusable).

Also: a staging buffer dropped while a submission may still read it is
kept alive through host::retire and never pooled (it was pooled at once,
which VICTORY_STAGING_POOL_MB would turn into a race).

Frame line: staging buffers (VICTORY_STAGING_DOUBLE) counts fresh
buffers made while busy, their bytes, submissions that still settled for
a staging buffer in flight, and buffers kept until their submissions
finished.

feat: GPU: staging memory cut from 64 MiB blocks (VICTORY_STAGING_BLOCKS=1)

Staging buffers were a committed upload buffer per texture, about 0.5 ms
each and 1,000-2,200 a frame in the opening cutscene. With
VICTORY_STAGING_BLOCKS=1 they are pieces of 64 MiB upload blocks, cut
on 4 KiB grain by ranges.rs. A piece goes back to its block when its
staging buffer is dropped; a buffer dropped while a submission may still
read it hands its piece to host::retire, so the range is reused only
after that submission has finished. Off by default.

Also: a staging buffer dropped while a submission may still read it is
no longer pooled at once (VICTORY_STAGING_POOL_MB), which was a race.

Frame line: staging buffers count pieces cut from blocks and the fresh
buffers of VICTORY_STAGING_DOUBLE.

feat: GPU: heap pass looks at the slots marked since its last pass (VICTORY_HEAP_PASS_DIRTY=1)

The pass over the heap's buffer views re-looked at every view (81,000
in the world) every 16 passes. With VICTORY_HEAP_PASS_DIRTY=1 a slot is
looked at again only when its buffer view was written or went, when the
title released the resource its record named (descriptor::forget), when
its 12-byte record in title memory changed, or when it found no host
copy (every 16 passes). Every 256 passes all slots are looked at again as
a safety net. The spans of host copies are worked out again only for
copies whose slots went. Off by default; the old pass stays the default.

Viewer: fixes from the whole-fleet check (wheels on two-wheelers, boats, placeholder colours)

A render of all 315 vehicles showed four faults in the viewer:

- Wrong wheels on bicycles and some motorbikes and cars. The viewer
  loads default wheels first; when those finished loading after the
  vehicle's own wheels had been requested, they were shown and the
  load counted as done. Finished loads now carry the rim|tyre key they
  were asked for and only the current one is used.
- Rim size on two-wheelers. They have no wheel fitment record. There
  wheelScale is the rim radius (0.217 on a BMX whose tyre is 0.268,
  0.254 / 0.223 on a dirt bike), so the rim ratio is wheelScale over
  the collision disc's radius when it comes out between 0.55 and 0.95
  and no fitment record gives one.
- Boats and other vehicles without wheel bones had no Vehicle panel, so
  no configuration or paint was ever applied and they showed the
  default red. Models with part colours get the panel too, and a
  screenshot waits for their data as it does for wheeled vehicles.
- Aircraft and two trailers were magenta: their configurations store
  pure magenta (ff00ff) where they have no body colour of their own.
  That value is skipped and the most frequent colour of the vehicle's
  first paint list is used.

Checked in the viewer: bmx, erode, scorcher and aphid (spoked wheels,
thin tyres), seashark in two configurations, tao, marquis, jet,
traileruld1.

GPU: the texture pass's time budget is the frame's, not each pass's

In the opening cutscene two passes over the heap's texture slots in one
frame took 750 ms each (the catch-up budget), a frame of 2.8 s. The time
the frame's passes have taken is now kept, and a later pass in the same

GPU: the guards' view blocks are bits read without their lock (the wide copy workers stood 206 ms a frame waiting for it)

Every asking about a range of title memory took the guards' lock to learn
whether its first block is view memory the guards hold (known_view, and
the same test at the start of guard()). The run 44 profile has the six
wide workers waiting 206 ms a frame together for that lock, most of it
there. A bit per 64 KiB block (title addresses below 1 TiB, 2 MB) is now
kept beside the guards under their lock and read without it; past the
bits the lock is taken as before. A stale bit only sends an asking the
old way: a block wrongly taken as a view is asked of the guards, which
find it is not one; one wrongly not taken as a view is asked of the
kernel, which fails, as before the bits.
Merge pull request #44 from Apenshot123: find free descriptor runs across the search cursor (victory-fork PR 932)

GPU: guard() asks the kernel where absent blocks' uncommitted memory ends before it takes the guards' lock

With the view blocks read without the lock (4885d09), the wide workers
still stood 229 ms a frame together waiting for the guards' lock in
guard() (profile of 26 November, the cell), and its holders were mostly
in NtQueryVirtualMemory: uncommitted_end, asked under the lock for every
region of absent blocks. The absent blocks are now bits too, kept with
the others; guard() asks the kernel about the regions of the absent
blocks of its range first, and under the lock uses those answers for
blocks its own set still holds absent. A remap meanwhile takes a block
out of that set under the lock, so a stale answer is never used for it.

GPU: staging slab heaps left empty are let go, not only those whose every slot was used once; the fullest heap is filled first

A slab heap was let go only once it had no buffer and every one of its
slots had held one: a heap of 256 slots of which 40 ever held a buffer
stayed for good. The laptop run of 26 November had 285 heaps of 16 MB
and 81 of 32 MB of upload memory with 38 MB of staging alive, about
2.4 GB more of the PC's memory in use than before the slabs, and 200 to
350 MB left free. A heap left with no buffer is now let go at a later
call, two empty ones kept in all, and a buffer goes into the fullest heap
of its size with a free slot, so that the others empty.

DirectStorage: read deferred zero mappings as native inputs

Kernel-native reads cannot invoke the first-touch handler. A valid untouched lazy page table or memory source therefore failed with E_ACCESS_VIOLATION. Prepare only still-reserved whole pages already tracked as lazy, then retry the normal read or validation, including when another thread already committed them. Other reservations and committed protections remain unchanged.

Six CPU regressions cover deferred memory sources, owned page-array snapshots across a page boundary, ordinary unreadable reservations, explicit readonly/noaccess/guard protection, partially committed pages, and a deterministic competing-first-touch race. The two positive cases fail on official dd2ae9a without the fix. Focused DirectStorage tests: 19 passed; existing lazy tests: 2 passed. No GPU or retail run in this change; relationship to the observed retail storage failures remains unproven.

D3D12.X: an allocator put aside keeps its recordings' memory (#1358)

A title's allocator Reset while the GPU still runs what was recorded on
it puts that PC allocator aside (alloc_pool, #897) and returns S_OK.
real::alloc_reset took the S_OK as "the GPU is done" and freed every
unified-memory block that ended recordings on the title's allocator had
used: root argument tables, io and AllocateUploadMemory blocks. Coherent
blocks go back on the pool's LIFO stack, so the next translated draw can
take one and write its arguments over those a submitted draw has not
read yet; sparse ones are decommitted. #897 counted 240 such swaps in
60 s of a retail title's world.

The blocks were also held under the title's allocator, which since #897
stands for PC allocators that change, so no one Reset could tell whether
the GPU was done with all of them.

A recording's blocks are now held for the PC allocator it is on (the one
alloc_pool's reset_list hands to the PC Reset), and alloc_pool gives a
PC allocator's blocks back at the title's Reset once the GPU has passed
every submit on it, whether it is in use, was reset or was put aside. A
PC allocator made here that is released gives its blocks back with it.

The device test through the Reset hook finds the blocks freed at the
swap on the old code (run on Wine's D3D12 over MoltenVK; no Windows
machine here).

Fixes #1358.

D3D12.X: shaders that index the heaps themselves get the heaps' addresses

A root signature with CBV_SRV_UAV_HEAP_DIRECTLY_INDEXED or SAMPLER_HEAP_DIRECTLY_INDEXED has the
console put the 32-bit address of the bound view heap / sampler heap into user SGPRs after the
root arguments, the view heap's first. XCL left these registers 0, so the shaders read their
descriptors from address 0 on.

Measured on a retail title: 110 of 153 root signatures at its first screen have one of the flags.
All 540 of its compute shaders with such a root signature that were built (218 with the view heap
flag, 3 with the sampler heap flag, 319 with both) have exactly one user SGPR more per flag than
their arguments take; those with both load T# from the first. The pixel shaders of 49 572 pipelines with the
sampler flag have one more as well (by where their m0 comes from). The pictures of its loading screen took a wrapping sampler
instead of the clamping one they ask for: a flickering line at their top edge.

D3D12.X: execute two-pass mesh shaders on DispatchMesh and ExecuteIndirect

Console mesh shaders translated to a two-pass pair (compute + mesh/PS,
TwoPassPso) were built by CreatePipelineState but had no execution path:
DispatchMesh was not hooked on the console command list vtable, and
ExecuteIndirect did not dispatch the compute pass or bind the record
buffer (u1) before invoking the mesh pass.

Hook DispatchMesh (slot 127, newer layout slot 129) and handle TwoPassPso
in ExecuteIndirect:
- Track console mesh root-argument layout (s[8:9] spill table, inline
  arguments from s16 across 16 SGPRs) in console_list::user_data_ms.
- Create a companion DISPATCH command signature alongside non-root-changing
  DISPATCH_MESH command signatures in device_x::create_command_signature_x.
- Allocate/recycle a DEFAULT-heap UAV record buffer per command list
  (recycled on allocator reset), bind u0 (io), u1 (res), u2..u5 (UMA),
  run the compute pass -> UAV barrier -> mesh pass -> UAV barrier, and
  scale indirect DispatchMesh group counts on the GPU when
  mesh_groups_per_record > 1.

Assisted-by: Antigravity (Gemini 4 Neon)

D3D12.X: give the two-pass io block the unified memory base

Without IO_UMA_BASE_HI the pair picked no memory window for any access.

D3D12.X: keep two-pass groups inside the record buffer

DispatchMesh runs at most the groups the buffer holds; ExecuteIndirect's
arguments are rewritten on the GPU with the same bound for both passes.

D3D12.X: run indirect two-pass groups of Y and Z too

Both passes index records by gid.x, so the rewritten arguments put x·y·z in X.

D3D12.X: read two-pass indirect arguments through memory, cap their scratch

The rewrite reads the commands through the memory window, not the title's buffer
in a guessed state, into shared scratch blocks capped at 16 MiB a recording.
Tests: cover a capped X-only two-pass indirect dispatch

D3D12.X: run a two-pass ExecuteIndirect one command at a time

Each command's records start at record 0, so its mesh pass draws them before the
next command's compute pass; commands past a count buffer's count get no groups.

D3D12.X: two-pass binds set the shared view heap first

kernelx: physical pages as section slices that can be mapped at many addresses

On the console a physical page mapped at several addresses is one page. XCL
keeps a page at one address at a time and copies it when the title maps it
elsewhere (`move_away`), so the other addresses go stale; a retail title maps
its streamed pages into a pool, into the CPU view of a 24 GB reservation and
into that reservation's GPU view (#1031).

`kernelx::sections` is the base for real aliasing: a block of physical pages
is one pagefile-backed SEC_RESERVE section, and a page is mapped as a view of
its 64 KiB slice into a placeholder (MapViewOfFile3 with
MEM_REPLACE_PLACEHOLDER). Every view of a slice is the same memory and a page
takes commit once, when it is committed through any view. Unmapping leaves a
placeholder for the next view. Ordinary reserved memory (write-watched if
asked) can replace part of a placeholder and go back to one.

Nothing calls it yet. Measured in a standalone program on Windows 11 26200
over 200 000 pages: map 2.2 us, unmap 2.75 us, commit 0.9 us a page.
GetWriteWatch refuses a range that holds a view (error 87), and one call
cannot span two neighbouring reservations either.
D3D12.X: add depth+UAV color twins and format-aliased placed texture copies

kernelx: catch CPU writes to the views of physical pages, page by page

The upload of title memory to video memory (`d3d12x::sparse`) and the
textures kept in step with title memory learn what the CPU wrote from the
write watch, and a view of a section (`kernelx::sections`) cannot be
write-watched: GetWriteWatch refuses any range that holds one.

`kernelx::guards` keeps the views of a physical page read-only. The first
write through any of them faults; a vectored handler makes that view
writable, notes the page and lets the write go on. `take_dirty` hands over
the pages of every view of each page written – a write through one view is
a write to all of them – and guards those views again before their bytes are
read, so a later write is caught again and an earlier one is in what is read.

Kernel calls do not fault into the handler, they fail: `lazy::ensure`, which
XCL already calls before a kernel call or its own code writes title memory,
opens the guards there first and counts the write. A view committed by the
lazy handler is writable and counts as written. Both take no lock until a
view has been watched.

Nothing watches a view yet.

kernelx: views of physical pages stay open across a write that cannot fault

A guarded view of a physical page (`kernelx::guards`) is read-only until it
is written. Code of XCL's own that writes there faults into the guard and
goes on, but a kernel call does not fault: ReadFile into such a view fails.
`lazy::ensure` opened the views first, yet the submit thread's `take_dirty`
could guard them again before the write – between DirectStorage's check of
its destination and the copy, or before the kernel wrote a ReadFile buffer.

`guards::open` now returns `Opened`, which keeps its views writable until it
is dropped; `take_dirty` uploads a pinned view but does not guard it again,
and the end of the write counts as a write. `lazy::ensure` returns it and its
callers hold it across their write: the routed ReadFile for a synchronous
read, and the destination checks of DirectStorage and the CPU-side
bottom-of-pipe writes. An overlapped ReadFile writes after the call returns:
its views stay open until its OVERLAPPED is no longer STATUS_PENDING, which
`take_dirty` reads without faulting (the title may free it once done). A
retail title reads 271 MB that way into the CPU view of its 24 GB
reservation 8.5 s after start.

`guards::written` counts a page as written through all its views when XCL
writes it by page number.

Nothing watches a view yet, so nothing changes without views.

kernelx: XCL_PAGE_ALIAS=1 shows a physical page at every address it is mapped at

Without it XCL keeps a physical page at one address at a time and copies it
when the title maps it elsewhere; the console shows the page at every
address it is mapped at. A retail title maps its streamed pages into a pool,
into the CPU view of a 24 GB reservation and into that reservation's GPU
view (#1031).

With `XCL_PAGE_ALIAS=1` (`kernelx::alias`):
- a block of physical pages is a section (`kernelx::sections`) with a view
  of its own, through which XCL reads and writes pages by number
  (DirectStorage); the title never maps a page there;
- the title's reservations of 64 KiB pages with no commit (its CPU view, GPU
  view and pool) are placeholders, and a page mapped there is a view of its
  slice, guarded (`kernelx::guards`) so that a write through one view is
  uploaded at all of them; `title_textures` adds those pages to what the
  write watch found;
- a page mapped anywhere else (a placeholder region the title made in a
  sparse window) is moved there and back with its bytes, as before.

Pages are committed on first use as before (`kernelx::lazy`); whether a page
is committed is a bit per page: asking Windows walked the rest of a fresh
block, and a title mapping 100 000 new pages one at a time took 20 s longer
to its first frame.

Measured in a traced run of a retail title: 3 blocks (11 360, 2 960 and
99 776 pages), 131 072 map calls in 150 s, nearly all single pages into its
plain reservations, none at a page's home, no commit inside them.

releasing a view drops its pages.

XCL keeps a physical page's data where it was mapped last, and the
title maps most streamed pages into the CPU view behind the GPU view
too, so `mapped_source` answers where that page is now (`page_now`),
else the pool page itself. Each title mapping is remembered per address
(Away::title), written once the page is in place and forgotten when the
reservation goes; a page freed while its allocation lives is no longer

DirectStorage: read a physical-page list again when its request runs

A retail title keeps its destination page lists in slots of its own
table and writes a slot's pages after EnqueueRequest. At enqueue such a
slot can still name the pages of the slot's previous request, and the
snapshot taken then is what execute() wrote to (#289 rereads only the
entries that are 0). Over 16 000 requests a run were written into pages
the title had since reused: its objects got garbage pointers and it
crashed about 20 s into world loading; when the old pages were freed,
the request failed with E_ACCESS_VIOLATION.

The console reads the list when it runs the request. execute() now
reads it again (through read_own, as the snapshot) and takes it when it
differs and every page in it is allocated (kernelx::physical_pages_live).
A list that was on the enqueuing thread's stack keeps the snapshot: that
memory is reused once the call returns, and a page ID written there
since can belong to another live allocation.

queues wait on which, but not what the GPU is running. With
XCL_GPU_CULPRIT=1 every dispatch XCL records (title lists,
console-recorded lists, ExecuteIndirect of a translated compute
pipeline) is wrapped in WriteBufferImmediate markers, in before and out
after, one pair of words per PC list in a readback buffer. At a release
the lists whose marker in is above their marker out are logged with the
dispatches between the two: console CS (fnv64 of the title's bytecode),
PC pipeline and groups.

On the retail title of #505 (RTX 5080) this named, at each stall, one
list with a run of 1-D dispatches of one CS whose first never finished;
not the same CS from run to run. DRED breadcrumbs were tried first: they
change the driver's pipeline cache keys, so every pipeline was built
again and the title never got past its start.

Off by default; without the variable nothing is recorded.

A console pixel shader compiled with [earlydepthstencil] runs with
DB_SHADER_CONTROL.DEPTH_BEFORE_SHADER (bit 12) set: depth and stencil

when it writes memory. XCL never read the register, so the PC ran such

on the HLSL path and ForceEarlyDepthStencil (shader flag bit 3) on the
direct DXIL path, which had it hard-coded to false. DXC accepts the
attribute together with an SV_Depth export.

The translator's source id covers these files, so cached translations
are made again.

polled before the list is submitted, while the write that satisfies it

no known value (fill, copy, a partial write, or a split segment), as
before. Otherwise it is recorded like any other wait.

D3D12.X: a dispatch put off to the submit waits there until it is built

With XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS set, a Dispatch or dispatching ExecuteIndirect put
off to the submit (#2118) was recorded through resolve_wait, with the same
budget a bind has as the title records. A pipeline a bind had already
found late got the stand-in at once, one still building got it after the
budget, and the dispatch was counted as skipped and left out. Its segment
lies between the list's other work, so the list's Write64 labels, EOP
writes and fence signals still fired: the title saw the work as done
while its UAV outputs, counters and indirect argument buffers were never
written.

record_deferred now waits for the segment's compute pipeline
(pso_async::wait_for_submit) before it records the call, whether a bind
found it late or not. Without the budget this is the wait the submit
already made. With it, the submit leaves the build to the workers for
the budget first, as a bind does, so big compiles keep their turns on
the workers; one no worker has started by then is built on the
submitting thread, so a submit never waits for a free worker. One a
worker builds is waited for at most 30 s (SUBMIT_WAIT_MOST, the time a
retail title's watchdog lets its main thread stand still, #891):
title_held stops kernelx::Sleep and the GPU-wait watchdog, not every
clock a title reads. Past that the call goes on with the stand-in as
before, with a WARN ("deferred dispatch skipped after waiting 30 s for
its pipeline") and a count of its own.

A worker's build that panics now ends as a failed build (catch_unwind
around the job), so whoever waits for it goes on instead of waiting for
a done flag nobody sets.

Tests: a put-off dispatch of a translated console program whose build
ends 400 ms into the submit, with a 50 ms budget and the pipeline already
late, has its store and the Write64 after it in the list reach memory
(without the change the label is written and the store is not); a
submit's wait for a late pipeline no worker can start builds it itself;
a submit waits for a worker's build no longer than its bound and counts
it; a panicking build ends as failed.

Recompiler: direct PS compares skip the per-quad mask where no helper bit is read

Since #2083 every pixel-shader compare on the direct route rebuilds its quad's four bits
from quad reads of its operands and four WaveActiveBallot passes. On 610 retail PS that
makes the DXIL 1.42x larger than before #2083; the driver time grew with it (+28 % to
+81 % on an RTX 4060, measured in #2083).

recomp/ps_masks.rs picks the cheapest form a compare's mask allows: the lane's own bit
when the mask is never read whole, WaveActiveBallot | own bit (HLSL ballot_px_local) when
it is read whole but nothing reads another lane's helper bit, cond ? EXEC : 0 for scalar
operands. In the ballot | own form every lane's copy of the mask has the live lanes' bits
and its own right, so EXEC predication, v_cndmask and carry-ins stay exact in helper lanes
and so do the values derivatives read later. A forward taint analysis refuses it where a
helper bit of another lane is read: a non-bitwise SALU, SCC / VCCZ, a scalar operand,
DPP / ds_swizzle / bpermute / permlane / readfirstlane while EXEC carries it, or values a
branch on such an EXEC lets differ between lanes. A subset of the entry EXEC (a kill's
live-pixel mask) has no helper bits and stays exact. Kept compares OR in their own bit.

610 PS: 43 % own bit, 31 % ballot | own, 4 % cond ? EXEC : 0, 23 % kept; DXIL x0.784
(x1.109 of before #2083), all validate.

alone. A mesh program never used its table at all.

float to its own component of its own element, in the VS outputs and in

register of a pair: the float16 registers pair up in order, so it is the
next one no other param starts with (f16_registers).

param of 383 packed params in 442 MS is exactly the predicted dwords.

A mesh program with a table now takes its params' registers from it,
float16 or not, as a VS already did; without one nothing changes.

Recompiler: scratch SADDR 0x7F addresses the offset alone (ST form)

RDNA2 scratch_* has three address forms, chosen by SADDR alone: an
SGPR is SS (SGPR + offset), NULL (0x7D) is SV (VADDR + offset) and
0x7F (EXEC_HI) is ST (the offset alone). There is no SGPR + VGPR form
and no SVE bit on RDNA2; both came with GFX11 / GFX940. This is how
LLVM encodes GFX10 scratch (FLAT_Real_gfx10 sets Inst{54-48} to EXEC_HI
for a scratch op without vaddr and to SGPR_NULL otherwise, and Inst{55}
to 0), and its gfx1030 MC tests encode `scratch_load_dword v1, off, off`
with byte 6 = 0x7f.

Both lowerings (direct DXIL lower_mem.rs and the HLSL emitter) took
0x7F for the SV form and added ADDR's VGPR, so an ST access went to a
per-lane address that its value happened to hold. They now use 0 as the
base for 0x7F, so ADDR is read only for 0x7D.

Issue #2400 proposed checking an SVE bit and adding SGPR + VGPR. The
RDNA2 ENC_FLAT_SCRATCH spec has no SVE field (bit 55 is not decoded),
so that half does not apply; the ST case it describes is real and is
the one fixed here.

Tests: an HLSL text check of the three forms and a direct DXIL check
that ST and SS containers do not change with ADDR while SV ones do
(both fail without the fix), a GPU test of the three forms, and the
existing scratch GPU test now encodes the SV form it describes.

Fixes #2400

D3D12.X: root views and indirect arguments in a GPU view ask for tiles

A retail title gives the GPU only addresses in a GPU view of its memory,
which with 16 windows lies in the view windows; a tile there gets video
memory only when an address in it is asked for (view_want). Nothing
asked yet: root CBV / SRV / UAV addresses read zeros, and a two-pass

uma_window_buffer has no buffer for one.

view window: 64 KiB each, as a root view has no size and nothing looks
a buffer up by address. The view windows' range is taken once, so any
other address costs one compare, and a layout without view windows one
compare a bind. The two-pass arguments and count, which only the GPU
reads, ask for their range and take the view window's buffer; the
indirect guard asks for the arguments it reads through the window; a
rect list in a view is expanded from its CPU view.

D3D12.X: lists take GPU-view addresses to their window and CPU view

With 16 windows an index or vertex buffer, a memory operation, a wait
or a copy destination can lie in a GPU view of the title's memory. The
PC got the console address of such a buffer when its window had no PC
address (no PC address: the device hangs), memory operations there were
"not in unified memory - not done", a wait read the view the CPU cannot
touch and passed at once, and a write and a wait naming the two views of
one value kept two sync cells.

Index and vertex buffers ask for their tiles and go to the PC at the
view window's address, or as none, never as the console address; the
CPU-side buffer mirrors never take a view address. Copies, fills,
immediates, timestamps and predication ask for their ranges and run on
the view window's buffer; what they and GPU copies into a buffer placed
in a view write is read back to the CPU view, where sparse lands it.
Waits read their value at the CPU view, and the sync cells are kept by
that address. Without view windows every address stays as it was.

Memory: tell sparse before a paired CPU view's pages are decommitted

The tiles of a GPU view in the view windows show the pages of its CPU
view: a submit fills them from those pages and scans them for changes
with the sparse state's lock held. Nothing told sparse when the title,
or XCL for it, decommitted or released such pages, so that read could
run on memory Windows had just taken away (the submit thread's copy
faulted that way once on a sparse window's pages).

  window's or unified memory's) calls sparse::source_decommitted for the
  range, the whole view on a release, before Windows does it; a decommit
  through VirtualFreeEx of a graphics reservation now takes that path.
- release_at, where a physical page leaves an address (unmapped, or
  moved to another), does the same for that page.
- mirrors::released, when a pair goes, has sparse forget the tiles over
  either view once its own lock is dropped (both addresses may be handed
  out again).

A count of pairs keeps it to one atomic load while nothing is paired;
sparse itself returns after one more while no tile shows a CPU view.

view are told while the pages are still committed, memory of no pair is
not, and the release forgets both views; a page mapped lazily into a CPU
view and written is found by the look (how sparse clears its hole), and

D3D12.X: keep CPU-view pages being decommitted as holes for submits

source_decommitted marked the pages of a CPU view as holes in the tiles
shown over it and dropped the state's lock; the caller's VirtualFree came
after, with no lock. A submit that took the lock in between still had a
page in its write-watch list, asked Windows again (still committed),
cleared the hole and scanned the page while VirtualFree landed (access
violation on the submit thread), or kept it committed in the tile for
good (later copies back, immediates and chunk checks touched it). A tile
asked for in that window was filled from such pages the same way. The
ANY_MIRRORS gate was check-then-act: a decommit that saw no mirror while
the first one was being linked was missed entirely.

A leaf lock (Sources) now holds a copy of the CPU runs that tiles show
(changed with src_runs) and the page ranges whose decommit is under way.
source_decommit / source_release bracket the caller's OS call: the range
is listed, the state is told only when tiles show the range, the OS call
runs with no XCL lock, then the range is unlisted (a release forgets the
tiles first). Submits link a tile before they ask Windows about its CPU
tile, and take listed pages as holes (holes_now, in map_mirrors,
mirror_writes and buffer_tiles), so through the one lock either the
decommitter sees the link or the submit sees the range. A tile is looked
up again once linked, so a forget_mirrors that found nothing linked and a
link after it cannot miss each other; the leaf's runs replace ANY_MIRRORS.
source_decommitted and forget_mirrors keep their signatures.

which only marked the entries keyed by the decommitted addresses (the

addresses, kept the pages as committed, so the next copy back, immediate,
chunk check or scan through them touched decommitted memory.

any tile shows CPU memory. decommit(a, n, os) brackets the caller's

D3D12.X: build every lazy graphics pipeline ahead of its first use

A retail title creates its ~2 700 pipelines in its first 6 s. With lazy
pipelines each got a stand-in and was built only at its first bind, or
ahead of it when an earlier run had used its shaders. Pipelines new to
the run were bound up to ~140 s after they were made, and each such draw
waited 7 - 15 s for translation, DXC and the driver; the title records
about one draw between two of them, so 14 pipelines meant 156 s without
a frame.

The lowest-priority preload workers now keep a backlog of every lazy
graphics pipeline: those of earlier runs first (as before), then all
others are translated and compiled by DXC (no driver memory kept, and the
disk caches hold them for the next run), then built by the driver one by
one. The title gets the same pipeline, only earlier.

- A pipeline a bind wants is not taken from the backlog: the workers
  build it, and a bind's wait still raises a backlog worker building it.
- A huge driver compile of a pipeline nobody has used yet waits behind
  any other build waiting for a slot (big_compile_turn): one a bind gave
  up waiting for goes first. Gate size and commit headroom are unchanged.
- Pipelines of no earlier run wait in the backlog while less than 8 GB
  of commit is free; at most XCL_PSO_AHEAD (default 4096) of them are
  built by the driver ahead (each keeps ~400 KB there); XCL_PSO_AHEAD=0
  turns it off. Compute pipelines, and pipelines with no shader key, are
  still built at their first use.
- The pipeline line counts pipelines translated ahead and the backlog.

D3D12.X: XCL_GFX_PSO_WAIT_MS bounds a draw's wait for its pipeline

Draws wait for a pipeline still being built until it is there: on a cold
cache a logo and UI text drawn once and kept were missing when they did
not. A retail title's world draws waited 7 - 15 s each for pipelines
built one after another, and no frame came for 156 s; while a bind waits,
kernelx stretches the title's long sleeps too.

XCL_GFX_PSO_WAIT_MS=<ms> (unset: wait as before) bounds the wait of a
draw for a graphics pipeline: after it the draw goes on with the stand-in
(it draws nothing), and the later draws of that pipeline do not wait
again until it is built - what XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS does for every pipeline.
Compute pipelines are still waited for without a limit: a skipped
dispatch would corrupt data for later work. It is decided in pso_async,
which knows the kind of the pipeline: the binds are unchanged.

A bind's wait marked the build wanted for good, so a build nobody waited
for any more still skipped the huge-pipeline gate and ran at a normal
priority: with time-outs, many big driver compiles could run at once.
The wanted mark is now a count of waiting binds; one that runs out of its
budget leaves it, and the build goes back behind the gate and to the
lowest priority on a preload worker. Having been used, it still goes
before the builds ahead of first use.

D3D12.X: a range a thread asked for lately is not asked for again

Vertex and index buffers and root views are asked for at every bind, on
the thread that records the list, and a title binds the same ones for
draw after draw. Each ask walked every 64 KiB tile of the range through
a shared set (sparse::map_mirror). A thread now remembers its last 8
ranges with the generation of the GPU views they were asked in, and a
view that goes or comes empties that memory (its tiles are forgotten
with it). The counters keep every call; the bytes count when a range is
new to its thread.

Acceleration-structure views get a path of their own in the counters.

D3D12.X: drop copies back recorded before a mirrored tile's memory changed

A copy back recorded its tile's CPU address and landed if the tile still
had that address; an immediate compared nothing. When a page of the CPU
view behind a tile was decommitted and committed again (or the view was
released and paired anew at the same address) before the copy landed,
the submit re-validated the page with sent = None, and land_page wrote
the GPU's old bytes into the new memory's zero chunks (or over chunks
already sent). An immediate recorded before a repoint was stored into the
new CPU view. Finished readbacks were also drained only after
map_mirrors / mirror_writes, so a page that stopped being a hole in that
submit took what the GPU had in it.

TileEntry gets a generation: new for each tile over a CPU view, and again
whenever a page of it becomes a hole. Copies back and immediates record
it and land only into an entry with the same one. Tiles of the window's
own keep generation 0, so their landings behave exactly as before. The
finished readbacks are now drained before the tiles change at a submit.

show it, run the call with no lock held and unlist it after: the sparse

buffer_tiles ignored new_mirror's result. At XCL_MIRROR_MB a GPU-view tile
of a placed buffer was refused, left out of the buffer's tile list, and
the buffer's reserved resource kept a NULL tile there for good, while a
later CPU write gave the window tile its own video memory: the two views
of one address disagreed. new_mirror also checked the cap before taking a
tile back from parked / kept, so a tile kept mapped for a placed buffer
was refused after its CPU view was committed and written again, and
stayed mapped in the window and the buffer with the old bytes while the
new ones never went up.

passed by buffer_tiles, and takes a parked or kept tile back before the
cap is looked at: that memory is held already.

D3D12.X: give refused GPU-view tiles video memory once there is room

A tile refused at XCL_MIRROR_MB stayed linked and in MIRROR_ASKED, so
asking again did nothing, and map_mirrors skipped linked tiles: the only
retry was mirror_writes, on a later CPU write to its CPU tile. Data the
title wrote once before the link (meshes, tables) never reached the GPU,
even after decommits and releases brought the room back. A tile for
which take_tile found no video memory was not even recorded, so a short
spell of VRAM pressure zeroed it for good. And while at the cap, every
submit that wrote a refused tile's CPU tile asked Windows about it again
under the state's lock, only to refuse it again.

new_mirror now records take_tile failures in `refused` too (counted once,
and for a second after one no other tile tries to make a heap unless a
tile is at hand). map_mirrors ends with retry_refused: when there is room,
up to MIRROR_ASKS_MAX refused tiles still linked and without memory get
one batched hole query and video memory (a fill of their CPU view); those
with no committed page leave `refused` for the write path. mirror_writes
skips refused tiles while there is no room or memory for them.

D3D12.X: bound the GPU-view fills of a submit by committed bytes

map_mirrors took up to 4096 asked tiles a submit and gave each video
memory at once, so a burst of asks filled up to 256 MiB at the next
submit: every committed page hashed and pushed through the 64 MiB
staging ring (waiting on the GPU for ring room) on the title's
submitting thread with the state's lock held, while its loading threads'
commits and decommits waited for that lock.

Asked tiles are now linked as before (their CPU tiles are watched from
then on) and queued in `later`; map_mirrors fills from the front of that
queue until XCL_MIRROR_FILL_MB of committed pages (16 MB by default) went
this submit, counting the pages a tile's CPU tile has committed, not
tiles. The rest wait for the next submits in their order: new asks are
taken in only once the queue is empty, and refused tiles go through the
same queue when there is room again, so a burst is not overtaken by
later asks.

The compute pass of a console mesh program writes each thread's position,
parameters and primitive into the group's record: slot = the thread's
index, with room for max_vertices vertices and max_primitives primitives.

follows it. The record buffer is a root UAV, so that is a store to an

time-out. Two reviewers of the two-pass path named this store as the one
shader access there that nothing bounds; it is not shown that it was the
access that faulted.

limit of the part it writes: the direct DXIL one (kernel::mesh_init /
Lw::mesh_export, which the compute pass uses) and the HLSL one.

D3D12.X: make the shared view heap 2^21 and fill unused slots with nulls

Translated shaders take a texture's index in the shared shader-visible
heap from a T# they read from memory and accept it when it is below
2^21 - 1. The heap was made at MaxViewDescriptorHeapSize (1 000 000 on an
RTX 5090, also the fallback when the query fails), so an index between
that and 2^21 passed the shaders' guard and read a descriptor past the
heap's end: memory the GPU has not mapped. Since the shaders read real
descriptor data from the title's memory, stale or garbage T#s reach that
path.

The heap is now tried with 2^21 descriptors first (resource binding tier
3 hardware takes more than the query says) and made at the queried size
only when that fails; a heap below 2^21 is logged as a warning that names
the uncovered index range. D3D12 leaves a new heap's descriptors
undefined, and only descriptors 0..MEM_HEAP_BASE were null views: every
descriptor past them now gets a null view (even SRV, odd UAV, as a
console slot's pair), copied from a CPU-only heap of 4096 once at
creation (2^21 copies, 64 MiB at a 32-byte increment; the time is in the
creation's log line). A range released by an unregistered heap gets null
views again before it can be handed out, since its views may name
resources that are gone. The heap is made and filled without GLOBAL
held: the adopted device's descriptor hooks look up the console heaps.

Cost: once at the first view heap (the fill), one copy per released
page range; nothing per draw or bind. The heap takes 2^21 instead of
1 000 000 descriptors of video memory.

D3D12.X: never bind a pipeline under a state that does not fit it

Four ways a draw reached the GPU with a pipeline and a root signature or
draw kind that do not belong together:

- DispatchMesh and ExecuteIndirect resolved the pipeline with
  resolve_wait and then again in two_pass_of. With a wait budget the
  first can give the stand-in and the build can finish before the
  second: the two passes were recorded with the stand-in as the mesh
  pass's pipeline under the two-pass root signature. The draw now
  decides once (draw_pipeline): the two-pass entry of exactly what
  resolve_wait gave (real::two_pass_entry, no second resolve), else the
  stand-in of a pipeline being built or built since (skipped, as a
  pending one was), else the rest as before.
- ExecuteIndirect with a built two-pass pipeline and a signature that is
  not a noted DispatchMesh one (one that changes root arguments, or
  whose companion Dispatch could not be made) fell through to the PC
  call under the title's root signature, with the pass-through mesh
  pipeline on the list reading root views that signature lacks. Skipped
  and counted, warned the first 4 times.
- A Draw whose pipeline resolves to a two-pass one (a console VS+GS)
  took the PC branch: a Draw on a mesh pipeline. Skipped, warned once.
- The PC branches bound the title's root signature only when one was
  set; without one the PC call ran under whatever a translated draw left
  (XCL's ABI or the two-pass root signature). Such a draw is now skipped
  (warned the first 4 times), except on a bundle, which takes its
  caller's, and an ExecuteIndirect dispatch, which does not use it. Two
  tests set the root signature a title sets after Reset.

lookup per mesh draw, one TWO_PASS lookup per draw with an untranslated
pipeline); nothing on translated draws.

D3D12.X: with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 split a look's time by what its calls found

The 256-look line says how long a look for CPU writes takes, not
whether that time is the walk over memory nobody wrote or the pages
taken (each a page-table entry changed and flushed). The two call for
different fixes: looking at less memory, or taking fewer pages.

XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 times every write-watch call of a look on the thread
that submits and adds them up apart for the calls that returned no page
and those that returned some: time, bytes covered, pages, calls. A line
every 256 looks:

  look split (256 looks): X ms a look in N calls over G MB that found
  nothing + Y ms in M calls over H MB with P pages

It answers the study's first question: what a look's time is made of.
XCL_LOOK_STATS=1 prints what it printed before; with the switch off a
look costs one more atomic load per write-watch call.

D3D12.X: null the shared heap's views of a resource when it is destroyed

A title keeps T#s, each with an index into the shared shader-visible view
heap, in its own memory, and its shaders read them from there. On the
console a T# of a released texture still names memory (leftover bytes,
nothing faults), so a title can sample a texture it has released (a
material table not updated yet, a sample of weight zero). On the PC the
heap slot kept the descriptor of the resource XCL destroyed: a shader
that samples it touches an unmapped address on the shader units. Nothing
cleared a slot when its resource went.

console_heap now remembers, for each index of the shared heap, the PC
resource its descriptor names (8 bytes an index, made with the first
view: 16 MiB for 2^21), and for each resource the indexes that named it
(entries may be stale; the per-index value is the truth). A view
published from CreateShaderResourceView / CreateUnorderedAccessView
(and the _at forms, which go through them) sets it, a copy between
console slots carries the source's, a null fill clears it. Right before
the PC object is destroyed - in late_release's drain before the real
Release of a held resource, and after the last Release of one that was
not held - every index that still names it gets the null view of its
kind (SRV at even, UAV at odd indexes); an index overwritten since by a
view of another resource is left alone. One lock (SLOT_WRITES) orders
the descriptor writes and the nulls, so a null never lands on a view
another thread just wrote; the copies under it go past the adopted
device's descriptor hook, which looks up the console heaps.

Cost: per view published, a lock, a descriptor copy (as before), an
atomic swap and, when the slot named another resource, a push to a
sharded map; per descriptor copy of n slots, n more slot lookups. Per
resource destroyed, one sharded-map lookup, and a copy per view it
still has. Nothing on draws or binds. Logged at the first 16 releases
that nulled any view and at powers of two.

D3D12.X: with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 split the scan from its gather and pool

submit_cost's "scan" is the time from the sparse lock's work to the
uploads: building the slots of the written pages (the gather) and the
chunk scan of those pages, which is shared with the worker pool. Which
of the two it is, and whether the pool helps at all, decides whether
the scan wants a cheaper gather, more workers or workers that are
awake.

worker_pool::run now says who did a job's items (the caller, the
workers) and how long after the job was handed out the first worker
took one. With XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 the submit's gather and scan are timed
apart, and a line every 256 looks says:

  scan split (256 looks): gather A ms, scan B ms a submit; of N items a
  job the caller did C %, the first worker began after D µs (J jobs in
  S submits, W with a worker)

It answers the study's question of what the scan's time is made of and
whether the shared scan is shared. Nothing changes in what the pool or
the scan do; with the switch off a submit costs one atomic load more.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: keep two-pass buffers of a recording with no allocator for 10 s

hold_res_until_reset returned at once for allocator 0, which dropped the
recording's two-pass record and argument-scratch buffers: their last
reference went while the list that writes them through root UAVs might
not have run yet (a list XCL never saw reset, a reclaimed segment reset
onto none). A released committed buffer's GPU address is unmapped, and
the compute pass's stores and the mesh pass's loads through it fault.

They are now kept with the time they were handed over and go to the
reuse pool (or are released) once 10 s old, looked at whenever an
allocator's buffers are released. No fence or allocator says when the
GPU is done with them, so time does, far past any frame in flight. At
most 1 GiB is kept; past it the oldest go early and that is logged
(first 4 times).

Cost: one more lock at each allocator's release of two-pass buffers;
nothing per draw.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 split the submit's sparse lock time

What submit_cost calls "sparse lock" is the wait for the sparse
state's lock and all the work done under it before the scan: landing
the finished copies back, the tiles over CPU views, the mappings sent
and the unmappings. A long wait asks for less work under the lock on
other threads; a long part asks for less of that part on this one.

With XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 each step is timed, and the tiles mapped (with
the calls), the tiles unmapped and the bytes of copies back landed are
counted. A line every 1024 submits, averages a submit:

  sparse lock split (1024 submits): wait W ms, copies back L ms (B KB),
  GPU-view tiles M ms, mappings P ms (T tiles in C calls), unmappings
  U ms (V tiles), rest R ms a submit (of S ms)

It answers the study's question of what "sparse lock" is made of. With
the switch off a submit costs one atomic load more, and each map or
unmap call and copy back a relaxed add.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: read ExecuteIndirect counts through a window only when they fit

The ExecuteIndirect count check reads the 20 bytes of an argument record
through a raw root UAV at the window address of the title's buffer.
uma_va_of checks only that the start lies in a window. A buffer in a GPU
view may run across a view window's end, and the view windows are
separate 4 GiB resources: a record straddling the end was read past
window k's buffer, an SM load from an address nothing maps (root views
have no bounds).

The record is now read through the window only when all 20 bytes are in
it (uma_window_buffer_gpu, as make_scaled_args_buffer does); otherwise
the program reads the title's own buffer, as it does for an address that
is not in a window.

Cost: one window lookup per checked ExecuteIndirect (max 1, no count
buffer).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: bind vertex and index views only up to their window's end

The title's GPU view is one range, but on the PC its windows are
separate 4 GiB buffers whose addresses are not adjacent. pc_va_in maps
only the start address: a vertex or index buffer view (or DrawIndexedX's
indices) that crosses a window's end was handed to the PC with the
title's SizeInBytes, so the input assembler could fetch past window k's
buffer into addresses no resource covers.

IASetVertexBuffers, IASetIndexBuffer and DrawIndexedX now clamp
SizeInBytes to the end of the window the address is in (warned once);
the GPU reads zeros past a view's size. A view inside one window is
unchanged.

Cost: per vertex / index buffer bind, a window lookup (arithmetic); the
title-memory lookup (a lock) only for a view that crosses a window end.

D3D12.X: with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 add up the submitting thread's frame

When one thread makes every submit and every present, a frame's time
on it is its submits, its presents, its waits for the frame event and
its waits on fences. submit_cost says what the submits cost; nothing
said what the rest costs on that thread, so a frame's budget could not
be added up, nor could the calls XCL counts already (placed textures,
physical page calls, ...) be told apart from other threads'.

api_cost remembers the thread of the first title submit seen (with
XCL_LOOK_STATS=2) and counts every call on that thread apart as well.
New entries, timed with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 only: the title's
ExecuteCommandLists as a whole (not XCL's own submits inside one or
inside a present), presents (PresentX, and the fallback's at a console
method) with their wait for the copy of the frame before apart,
WaitFrameEventX, and the copies back settled when a title thread looks
at a fence. The entry for the title's blocking fence waits is there for
the fence hook to use. With XCL_ACTIVITY, every 2 s:

  calls of the submitting thread (2 s): N ExecuteCommandLists in X ms,
  N presents in X ms, ...

It answers the study's question of where a frame's time goes on the
thread that submits outside the submit hook. The all-threads line is
unchanged with the switch off; a call XCL already counted costs one
atomic load more.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: unpin a placed buffer's tiles when its PC object really goes

res_release called sparse::forget_buffer, which unpins a placed buffer's
tiles, at the title's last Release, also when late_release kept the PC
object alive until the queues are past the work in flight. The kept
object still maps those tiles: sparse could hand them to another address
or retire the pool heap under them while work queued through the buffer
had yet to run. late_release's drain ends the object through the
original Release, which never told sparse. forget_buffer now runs from
res_release only for an object that is not held, and from late_release
right before the real Release of a held one. Right before, not after:
after it, another thread can make a buffer at the same address, whose
tiles this would unpin (the queues are past the work by then, and
forget_buffer takes no late_release lock and does not wait for the
sparse state's).

The same reuse made the address-keyed removals in res_release unsafe
when its Release had already ended the object (late_release off, or two
releases of the last two references at once): a resource made at the
address in between lost its UMA_BUFFERS / BUFFER_DELTA / TITLE_ADDRESS
entries and its pinned tiles. The last reference is now told by the
count after an AddRef and Release of our own (1: ours alone) on every
path, and the removals, the null views and, with late_release off, the
unpinning run while the object is alive, before the Release that ends
it. Of the two fixes the finding proposes this is the smaller: an
identity guard would need a generation in sparse's buffer table. What
is left is two threads releasing the last two references at the same
instant: both see 2, and the one whose Release ends the object cleans up
after it, as before.

Cost: none on draws or binds; per resource Release, the AddRef and
Release that late_release already made, now also with
XCL_LATE_RELEASE=0.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: with XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 count stale looks and XCL's own writes

Two things bound what a cheaper look could leave out or save.

A look takes the blocks written lately only; a write to another block
waits for the walk thread to find it. With XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 every look
counts whether the walk had made a block hot since the look before
began (a block no look had taken: written up to a walk pass ago), and
the walk times its passes over all watched memory.

XCL writes the title's memory itself: copies back landed and
immediates stored. The write watch reports those pages like the
title's, so a look takes them and the scan goes over them for nothing.
With XCL_LOOK_STATS=2 those writes keep their pages (64 Ki at most,
under the sparse state's lock they are made with) until the next look,
which counts how many it found and how many of those the scan found
unchanged.

Lines every 256 looks:

  walk staleness (256 looks): K of N looks began with a block the walk
  found that no look had taken yet; a walk pass took A ms (B ms the
  longest, P passes)
  XCL's own writes (256 looks): W pages a look written by XCL since the
  look before (copies back landed, immediates stored), F of them in the
  look, S scanned, U % of those found unchanged

They answer the study's questions of how stale the hot-block look is
and how much of a look is XCL's own writes. With the switch off a look
costs one atomic load more, a copy back landed or immediate stored one
per page.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

D3D12.X: let XCL's own pipelines go only once the queues are past them

The pipeline objects XCL owns - the compute pass of a two-pass pipeline
(Drop for TwoPassPso) and the background-built real pipeline behind a
title's stand-in (pso_release) - were released the moment the title
released its pipeline. A list recorded before that and still queued or
running binds them (the two-pass draws bind both), and D3D12 asks that a
pipeline outlives the work that runs it: the GPU would fetch shader code
of a destroyed pipeline.

late_release now takes them as well: a batch entry is a resource or a
pipeline, and a pipeline is released (its COM Release) once every known
queue has passed a fence value signalled after the hand-over, by the
same thread and drains as resources. With XCL_LATE_RELEASE=0 they go at
once, as before. Pipelines XCL releases that were never bound (a build
nobody waits for any more, a duplicate depth-bias pipeline) still go at
once; the depth-bias pipelines derived from a released base pipeline
(device_x) are not changed here.

Cost: a lock and a push per such release (a title's pipeline release);
nothing on draws or binds.

- a thread that looks for a removed device ten times a second (it was only

Direct DXIL: leave a group barrier of several hardware waves to the HLSL path

The direct translator turned s_barrier into a plain group barrier. That
barrier waits for every hardware wave of the group, and a console wave that
has left, or that ran one barrier fewer, never arrives: on the console the
waves left go on, on NVIDIA they wait for ever and the GPU hangs. The HLSL
path has had the barrier that counts the waves still there since 0c02b87
(xcl_s_barrier); with XCL_DIRECT_DXIL=1 compute programs and the compute
pass of mesh pipelines did not get it.

A retail title has it in 216 compute programs (19 of them branch a wave
with no active lane around barriers the other waves run) and in all 36 of
its mesh programs: the first wave of a group whose vertex or primitive count
is 0, or past 128, runs a barrier the other waves branch around, then the one
they all run. Its world, the first to draw meshes in two passes, ended in a
driver time-out with no shader exception in two runs of three.

A compute or mesh program with s_barrier in a group of more than one
hardware wave is now an error of the direct translator, which sends it to the
HLSL path (XCL_SAFE_BARRIER=0: as before, in both translators).

Not run on a GPU: whether this was the cause of those time-outs is not
shown, and the HLSL compute pass of that title's mesh pipelines has not run
in its 16-window layout.

D3D12.X: give shader-visible sampler heaps a PC sampler at every index

Translated shaders index the bound sampler heap with S# word 3 & 0x7FF
(SamplerDescriptorHeap in the HLSL path, SAMPLER_HEAP_MASK in direct DXIL),
so an index from 0 to 2047. A console sampler heap got as many PC samplers
as the title asked for (128 in a retail title): an S# the title builds itself
with a nonzero border color pointer in word 3 [11:0], or any index from 128
on, read past the end of the bound PC sampler heap, which D3D12 leaves
undefined.

A shader-visible console sampler heap now gets 2 048 PC samplers (the D3D12
maximum for a shader-visible sampler heap) whatever the title asked for, all
of them made as the zero sampler XCL already wrote into the title's slots
(point, wrap, mip 0). The console side does not change: the heap keeps the
title's slot count, its 16-byte increment and its indexes, and copies,
CreateSampler and the release only touch the title's slots. A CPU-only
sampler heap keeps the title's count (shaders never bind it). The cost is
up to 2 048 CreateSampler calls and 2 048 PC sampler descriptors a heap.

The PC heap's own GetDesc (not hooked) now says 2 048 for such a heap; a
console view heap's already says twice its slots.

Tested on the software adapter only (WARP): the new test
every_sampler_index_a_shader_forms_is_in_the_pc_heap checks the count for
every index a shader forms and that D3D12 makes a shader-visible sampler
heap of that size. Not run on the hardware GPU or on a title.

D3D12.X: remember the tiles a thread asked for in GPU views, not exact ranges

view_want's per-thread memory of the ranges it asked for lately matched an
exact (va, len) among the last 8. Mesh-stage root views of a retail title
come at a new offset of tiles asked for already, draw after draw, so
12 000-74 000 of them every 2 s missed it and walked their tiles again in
sparse::map_mirror (a shard lock and a hash insert a tile) for nothing.

The memory now holds the span of 64 KiB tiles each range covers, 32 of
them, and a range is skipped only when all its tiles lie in one span
asked for while the GPU views were as they are now: it is still emptied
when kernelx::gpu_view_map_gen() changes, and a range reaching one tile
further still goes to map_mirror. What gets mapped does not change.

map_mirror returns how many tiles it queued, and the "KB new" figure of
the "GPU view (2 s)" line counts those tiles (64 KiB each) instead of the
length of every range that missed the memory: before, 0.3-35 % of it ever
became a filled tile.

D3D12.X: keep a compute pipeline's driver blob from a 20 ms build on

The compute path kept a driver blob on disk only when its build took
250 ms (driver_cache::KEEP), and XCL_PSO_DISK_CACHE_MIN_MS, which the
graphics and two-pass paths read, did not reach it. A compute program
whose build takes 100 to 250 ms was compiled again in every run, at its
first bind, and a compute pipeline is waited for: often on one of the
title's threads. In a retail title's run one of its threads spent 228 ms
in the driver on a 4 KB program that no file was kept for.

driver_cache::keep (its only caller is translated_compute_pso) now keeps
a blob of a build of 20 ms or more, and XCL_PSO_DISK_CACHE_MIN_MS chooses
for it as for the others. The graphics and two-pass default stays 250 ms.
The cost is more small files in the driver folder, at most one a compute
program. Programs under 16 KB of DXIL still keep no blob
(COMPUTE_BLOB_MIN_DXIL), as before.

100 ms compute build and fails on the old threshold. Not run on a GPU or
on the title.

Direct DXIL: one split console wave of a compute or mesh group exchanges by counters

A wave64 program on 32-lane hardware runs as two hardware halves that
exchange ballot words and lane values. Groups of more than one console wave
do that through bounded group-shared counters; a group of exactly one
(33 to 64 threads) met at a group barrier at every exchange. Those barriers
hung NVIDIA GPUs when several such programs ran at once (#1727: device hung
and driver event 153 in 11 of 25 parallel runs of the lib tests on an
RTX 5070, none on the HLSL path, whose exchange spins by default). A retail
title's world runs such programs on several queues at once and ended in a
driver time-out with no shader exception.

A compute or mesh group of one console wave now takes the counter exchange
too (its slots and counters are made for it when the program has no LDS).
Geometry programs, which set their partner by phase, and the tests' kernel
form keep the barrier. The change is that of #1741 (hajduzsolt), which is
open and written against an older main; applied here by hand.

Not run on a GPU. The test checks the translated program: one group barrier
(the start's) and the counters' atomics for 33, 64 and 128 threads.

D3D12.X: size two-pass record buffers in powers of two and keep freed ones

A retail title's world made about 33 committed buffers of 1-32 MiB a second
for two-pass mesh draws, and let as many go, on a card that was nearly full
(the "two-pass res buffer #n" lines: #2048 at 201 s, #8192 at 384 s). Most
of them are 32 MiB, and they do not come from DispatchMesh: an
ExecuteIndirect of two-pass commands always asked for 32 MiB of records
(each with a 1 MiB argument scratch block), since a command's groups are
known on the GPU only. A DispatchMesh asked for its need, at least 4 MiB.

Each recording keeps its buffers until its PC allocator is reset; then they
went to FREE_RES, which kept 16 buffers or 256 MiB at most: eight of the
32 MiB ones. 24-27 of them were made in the world's first two seconds, so
each round of allocator resets let go of most of what the next recordings
made again. The pick from FREE_RES also took the
first buffer large enough, so a DispatchMesh of a few groups could take a
32 MiB one that the next ExecuteIndirect then made anew.

- Record buffers are a power of two from 1 MiB (the scratch block's size)
  to 128 MiB. A draw gets at least the groups it got before (a test checks
  this over record sizes, splits and group counts). An ExecuteIndirect keeps
  32 MiB of records unless a command's groups in X (65 535 / split) need
  less, which leaves its group cap as it was.
- FREE_RES keeps every buffer handed back, up to 1 GiB, and lets go of one
  no recording took for 2 s; a recording takes the smallest one that fits,
  the last handed back of that size. What it keeps is bounded by what
  recordings took in the last 2 s and by 1 GiB.

When a buffer goes back to FREE_RES does not change: when its allocator is
reset (or alloc_pool sees the GPU past its submits), or 10 s after a
recording with no known allocator. A buffer leaves FREE_RES only for a
recording or to be let go, both after that point.

The DispatchMesh floor goes from 4 MiB to 1 MiB: fewer bytes past the last
record. Every store to a record is bounded by its vertex and primitive
counts (HLSL and direct DXIL mesh and geometry paths), so a store does not
reach past the records a draw dispatched.

Tested on the software adapter only (unit tests of the sizing and of the
pool). Not run on a GPU or with the title: how many buffers a frame now
makes is not measured.

Memory: size the coherent window from what the heaps setting puts in it

The coherent window is committed when unified memory is made, so it is
sized from what the title asked of it in an earlier run
(<data>/cache/uma_coherent.txt), and that value only grew. A retail
title's 4582 MB of GPU heaps, stored by a run that put them in the
window, made two coherent windows of 4095 + 998 MB in later runs with
XCL_COHERENT_HEAPS=sparse:16. Those runs sent every such heap to the
sparse windows and put at most 105 MB in the coherent window, but with
XCL_UMA_SHADOW=1 each window is shadowed by a video-memory heap of its
full size: about 4.6 GB of video memory and as much commit for nothing,
on a card that was full. The sparse branch returned before the need was
noted, so the stale value never came down.

uma_coherent.txt now keeps one size per XCL_COHERENT_HEAPS setting
(lines "<bytes> <setting>"; the old single number counts as the setting
that puts every heap in the window), and the window is sized from the
one of the run's setting. A heap sent to the sparse windows is noted
too, and a run that has lasted 60 s stores what it put in the window by
then even when that is less than the stored size. A run that ends
sooner only grows it, so a run cut short before it made its heaps does
not leave the next one a window too small for them. XCL_COHERENT_MB
still chooses the size.

With one coherent window instead of two, the view windows of the
16-window layout start at window 4 instead of 5. Everything that uses
them asks the layout (is_view_window, bind::view_span_of,
list_x::pc_va_in, real.rs), and the uma tests already build that layout
with a 512 MB window. Shader translation and the shader and driver
caches are keyed on the number of windows (pso::mem_windows), which
does not change.

Tested: cargo check -p xcl --tests; the uma and kernelx unit tests
(new: the_stored_coherent_need_is_the_one_of_the_heaps_setting,
coherent_heaps_routes), on the software adapter. Not run on the title
or on a hardware GPU.

D3D12.X: a view slot that gets no room in the shared heap names the null views

When the shared view heap is full, a page of a console view heap that is
first used gets no place there. console_heap::slot then gave its slots the
index 2k, the one they would have in a PC heap of their own, and XCL wrote
that index into the slot's T# (CreateShaderResourceView,
CreateUnorderedAccessView, copies). But that heap is CPU-only once it is
meant for the shared heap, and lists bind only the shared heap, so the
shaders read descriptor 2k of the shared heap: another heap's view, a memory
window's raw buffer UAV for k from 2 to 9 (read as a texture, which hangs
NVIDIA), or, for k of 500 000 or more in a large heap, a descriptor past the
heap's end that the translators' guard (below 2^21 - 1) lets through.

Such a slot now has index 0, the null SRV / UAV pair at 0 / 1, with no
shared descriptor and no GPU handle (nothing is copied for it, and a UAV
clear of it is skipped as before). A heap that has no shared heap at all
keeps its own PC heap and 2k. The frame-trace census takes 0 as such a
slot's own index. Every page that finds no room is counted (each try), and
the warning comes at the first and at every power of two with the count,
where it came only once before.

Nothing in the logs of the last three runs of a retail title shows the
shared heap full, so this does not explain them; that title's heaps would
need 2.56 times the shared heap if every page were placed.

Tested on the software adapter only: the new test
a_slot_whose_page_finds_no_room_names_the_null_views (a fake shared heap with
room for one page, run in a child process) fails without the change (slot
258 got index 516) and passes with it. Not run on the hardware GPU or on a
title.

D3D12.X: count two-pass buffers made, taken again, let go and alive

How many two-pass record buffers and argument scratch blocks were alive at
once was not logged: the analysis of a retail title's world had to work it
out from the addresses of the first 48 and the powers of two of "two-pass
res buffer #n", and could only guess their share of the 5 GB of video memory
the memory line does not name.

A two-pass buffer is now a TwoPassBuf that counts itself when it is made and
when it is dropped, wherever that happens (FREE_RES letting go of an idle
one or one past its cap, the no-allocator hold past its cap, a test). A line,
always on, at most every 2 s while the counts change:

  D3D12.X: two-pass buffers: N made, N taken again, N let go; N alive

D3D12.X: XCL_CS_PSO_WAIT_MS limits a dispatch's wait for its pipeline

A dispatch waits for its compute pipeline until it is built, and a bind
whose pipeline no worker has started builds it on its own thread, outside
the gate of huge driver compiles. A lazy compute pipeline is sent to no
worker before its first bind, so its first bind always builds it there. In
a retail title's run one of its threads spent 57 s in the driver's
compiler on one program no earlier run had used (827 KB of DXIL, no driver
blob), and another of its threads waited for that pipeline all the time:
no frame for 57 s.

XCL_CS_PSO_WAIT_MS=<ms> is a budget of compute pipelines, as
XCL_GFX_PSO_WAIT_MS is one of graphics pipelines (it goes before
XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS for them). With it a bind takes the path XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS
takes today (resolve_within): the build goes to the xcl-pso workers, where
a huge driver compile waits for its slot once no thread waits for it, the
bind's thread waits at most the budget and never builds the pipeline
itself, and past the budget the pipeline is late: its dispatches get the
stand-in until it is built. Dispatch, the console list replay and
ExecuteIndirect already skip a dispatch with a stand-in and count it
(Dispatch and the replay as a skipped dispatch, ExecuteIndirect as a
skipped draw). Each late program is logged once ("compute pipeline of
record X not built after N ms: its dispatches are skipped until it is"),
by its console program's hash, which the pipeline now carries from its
creation.

Unset or 0, a compute pipeline is waited for exactly as before: the
budget is XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS, and without that, until it is built.

What a skipped dispatch breaks: what it computes is missing or old until
the pipeline is built. When that is the count of a later ExecuteIndirect
(culling and compaction programs), indirect_guard replaces only counts out
of range; an old count in range still draws or dispatches over old data.

Tested with the unit tests only (software adapter): the choice of the
budget, a bind that waits no longer than it while a worker (not the bind's
thread) builds a lazy compute pipeline, and one log line a program. Not run
on a GPU or on the title: what skipped dispatches do to its frames is not
known.

Memory: let freed sparse pool tiles cool for 2 s before they are reused

A pool tile that flush_parked unmapped went straight to the free list,
and take_tile popped it last in, first out: the tile unmapped last was
the next one mapped, cleared and filled for another address on the
"xcl sparse queue". When the free list was empty, take_tile even flushed
the parked tiles itself and took one of them in the same submit. That
queue waits for no title queue (with the readback queue, the normal
case), so work the title submitted before the unmap and still running on
its own queues could read the new owner's zeros or bytes, or write into
its tile through the old mapping. vram.rs keeps its freed pages cooling
for 2 s (COOL) for the same reason; sparse.rs had nothing of the kind.

Freed pool tiles (flush_parked, and release_if_unused when a placed
buffer's last user goes) now go to State::cooling with the time they
were freed. take_tile takes the oldest tile freed 2 s ago or more, then
one of the free list (tiles of a pool never used), and otherwise takes
back a retired pool or makes a heap: a tile freed less than 2 s ago is
never handed out, and take_tile no longer flushes the parked tiles (they
would only start cooling). retire_free_pools counts only free and cooled
tiles, so a pool with a tile still cooling is not retired.
new_mirror's "tiles at hand" check after a failed heap counts free,
cooled and retired tiles, no longer parked ones. pool_bytes counts the
cooling tiles as not mapped.

This is a time bound, not a fence: a GPU frame longer than 2 s can still
race. It holds more video memory while a title gives back and asks for
tiles (about 2 s of freed tiles, 60 MB at the 466 tiles/s measured).

Tested on the software adapter: cargo test --release -p xcl --lib sparse
(51 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored). New tests

a_pool_with_a_tile_still_cooling_is_not_retired (an injected clock), and
a_tile_given_back_is_not_used_again_before_it_cooled (a state on the
software device); all three fail with COOL set to 0.

here for the new rule, opens the hardware device and was not run. Not

D3D12.X: give back page pool heaps of title textures that came free

The 64 MiB pool heaps that back the 64 KiB pages of textures in title
memory (vram::Pages) only grew: bind made a heap when the pool had no
free tile, and nothing ever let one go. In two runs of a retail title
350 MB of those pools sat free, more after a streaming burst, on a card
that was full.

A pool heap all of whose tiles are free goes now. A tile is only in a
free list after COOL in the cooling queue, so such a heap has no page
in use, idle or cooling. After each placement, TilePool::take_free_heaps
takes such heaps out: their tiles are not handed out again, and their
index becomes free (TilePool::live, Pages.pools holds None there). The
next heap takes the first free index. take_batch now gives make_heap
the index to fill, so the pool and Pages.pools cannot disagree on it.
A tile of a given-back heap that came back to the pool (none should)
is dropped instead of handed out.

A heap that came free is retired first, as sparse.rs retire_free_pools
does with its pools. The next pool that is needed takes it back before
a new heap is made, so placing and freeing in turn does not make and
end a heap each time. It is let go once the page-mapping fence is past
the value it had when the heap came free and 2 s went by. Even then it
does not go at once: it goes through late_release (new: hold_heap,
Dead::Heap), in a batch sealed after it. A texture the title released
is held there and still maps pages of the heap, and work queued before
that release may still read them. A heap destroyed under that work is
a GPU page fault, where a page reused under it only gives wrong texels.
So the heap goes once every queue XCL knows of is past that work, never
before the textures held with it. If a queue never gets past, the heap
is never released, which is no worse than before.

The 'pools' figure of the memory line (page_bytes) counts the retired
heaps that are not let go yet.

tests on the software adapter (new: tile_pool_gives_back_wholly_free_heaps_and_reuses_their_index,
retired_pool_heaps_go_after_the_fence_and_a_moment). The test of the
churned pool now also checks the index each new heap gets. Not run: the

reservable_agrees_with_the_driver and the other hardware tests), the
