D3D12.X: build compute pipelines of new shaders ahead of their first use

The build-ahead backlog took a lazy compute pipeline only when an earlier
run had used its shaders (used-pipelines.txt). Any other compute pipeline
was built at its first bind, which waits for it: in a retail title's run
one of its threads spent 57 s in the driver's compiler on a program the
two runs before had never used, while another of its threads waited for it.

Compute pipelines of shaders no earlier run used now go to the backlog
too, in a lane of their own. The backlog serves the known compute
pipelines first, then this lane, then the known graphics ones, then the
other graphics ones (translated first, then built) as before. The known
compute ones, which used to share a lane with the known graphics ones in
the order they were made, now all come before them. The new lane is under
the rules of every pipeline no earlier run used: built only with
XCL_PSO_AHEAD's cap not reached and 8 GB of commit free (ahead_room),
counted against that cap, on the lowest-priority preload workers, a huge
driver compile behind the gate and giving its turn to any build a bind
waited for, and one a bind wants is left to the bind's workers.

This shortens how long a new compute pipeline is waited for (or, with
XCL_CS_PSO_WAIT_MS, how long its dispatches are skipped) and fills the
driver blob folder for the next run. It cannot build all of a title's
compute programs in its menus on a first run: a retail title has ~1 600
it never used, many of them taking the driver seconds to a minute.
The cost: each pipeline built keeps ~400 KB in the driver whether it is
used or not, and the known graphics pipelines are built later than
before, so a draw is more likely to wait for one (or, with
XCL_GFX_PSO_WAIT_MS, to be skipped).

The test of known pipelines built ahead no longer says an unknown compute
pipeline is still pending before its first bind (it may now be built
ahead); it still says nobody used it before then. Tested with the unit
tests only (software adapter): the lane order, room and cap, and a lazy
compute pipeline of new shaders built with no bind when commit is free.
Not run on a GPU or on the title.

D3D12.X: cap the bytes of two-pass buffers alive (XCL_TWO_PASS_MB)

Nothing bounded the two-pass record buffers and argument scratch blocks
alive at once: each recording holds its own until the GPU is done with it,
and a retail title's world had about 0.8 GB of them a few seconds in, on a
card its process kept nearly full. A committed buffer made there succeeds
above the OS budget, so nothing else would have stopped them.

A two-pass buffer is now made only if the bytes of those alive (held by
recordings, waiting for their allocator, or free) stay within the cap:
1024 MiB by default, XCL_TWO_PASS_MB to choose. When they would not, the free
ones in FREE_RES are let go first, oldest first, as many as it takes (the
GPU is done with them). If that is not enough, the buffer is not made and
the draw that asked for it is skipped, as one whose record does not fit the
record buffer is today, with a warning the first 8 times and a count on the
"two-pass buffers" line. The count is reserved before the buffer is made,
so threads making them at once do not pass the cap together.

Buffers held for a recording are never let go for the cap: when they go
does not change.

Tested on the software adapter only (unit test of the reservation and of
making room). Not run with the title: whether 1 GiB skips draws in its
world is not known.

retired once its last tile has cooled. retire_free_pools was still called
only right after flush_parked() freed tiles, and the tiles that flush
freed were stamped with its own instant, so they could never complete a

stayed (and retired heaps were not dropped) until some later give-back.

once per COOL after the last try (retire_due, retire_tried), so a submit
does not count the cooling queue every frame. A pool goes at most about

PARKED_MAX flushes while decommitting) are unchanged. Retiring later than
the flush uses a fence value at least as new as the one the flush signalled

D3D12.X: build new compute pipelines ahead on one worker at a time

The lane of compute pipelines no earlier run used, added two commits
ago, came before the known graphics pipelines with no bound: every
preload worker took from it while it held anything, and pipelines made
later joined it ahead of all queued known graphics ones. A retail title
makes ~1 600 compute pipelines it never used, some taking the driver a
minute, and there are 2 to 4 preload workers, with one huge driver
compile at a time behind the gate: all workers could sit on that lane
(one compiling, the others parked at the gate) for the whole session,
and no known graphics pipeline, not even one whose driver blob loads in
milliseconds, would be built ahead. Each would then be built at its
first draw on the title's thread. That commit's message said they are
built "later than before"; they could be starved.

Backlog::next now hands out one pipeline of that lane at a time
(compute_out, cleared by Backlog::built when the worker's build is over
or a bind took the job): while a worker builds one, the other workers
take the known graphics pipelines and the rest in the order as before.
The known compute pipelines still come first, and the lane is still
under ahead_room, ahead_cap and the gate.

Left out: when nothing else is queued the other workers stay idle
rather than build more new compute pipelines; the lane drains at one
worker's speed. A known huge graphics build can still wait at the gate
while the lane's build holds the only huge slot (XCL_HUGE_PSO_CONCURRENCY
default 1), as any two huge builds ahead of their use do.

GPU (the fences `executed` set) - the same test a Reset of it passes

allocator may be both its own stand-in and put aside, and its backing
goes at the first. Still left as before: an allocator a list still
records on at its Release, or whose submits the GPU has not passed,
keeps what it held (its backing is no longer tracked, so nothing says
when the GPU is done with it); the next commit logs those bytes so a

D3D12.X: only a whole texture upload seeds the stream recheck baseline

The stream recheck fingerprints a texture that is not fully write-watched
when it is uploaded, and re-queues it at later frame milestones when its
memory no longer matches that fingerprint. It assumed every upload sends
the whole texture, so the fingerprint equals what the PC texture holds.
Here an upload can be partial: a Due with whole == false sends only the
written pages it knows of, or nothing when texture_upload::changed finds
them unchanged. seed_stream_recheck seeded every Due, so after an
unwatched write followed by a partial upload of other pages the baseline
already held the unwatched bytes, the milestone recheck matched it, and
the texture kept the old contents on the GPU.

Only a whole Due now sets the baseline. A partial one leaves the entry
alone, its schedule too: moving the schedule on every partial upload would
keep a texture written every few frames from ever reaching a milestone.
A partial Due that turns into a full upload (Parts on a render target, or
XCL_TEXTURE_PARTS=0) does not reseed either; its milestone then sees the
old baseline and queues one extra whole upload.

The new test seeds with a whole upload, writes an unwatched byte, runs a
partial Due through the seeding and checks that the milestone queues the
texture; it fails without the change. Both stream recheck tests now take
TEST_LOCK, since a recheck in one checks the other's STREAM_RECHECK entry.

also removes the list's last submit and recording count, which
alloc_pool::in_flight reads: pop_spare then handed out a PC list the GPU
was still running, the title recorded into it and submitted it again
(debug layer id 553; NVIDIA removes the device), and note_resubmits had
nothing left to report it with. It happens with a stand-in moved to the
spares while its submit runs, a segment still queued behind a queue Wait
after the primary is done, and the segments KickoffX has just submitted.

clear_segment_state now calls alloc_pool::unpin_list, which removes only
the allocator pin (of_list and the backing's users). forget_list, which
removes everything, stays for the paths where the PC list is destroyed
(on_release, title_list::release) and its address can come back.

more while the queue is held, so a stand-in still in flight is in the

D3D12.X: a copy of a destroyed resource's view is the null view

When a PC resource is destroyed, resource_gone makes its views in the
shared shader-visible heap null views and records those indexes as
naming nothing. The title's own PC heap, the CPU-only mirror views are
made in and copied from, keeps the destroyed resource's descriptor. A
later copy of that console slot (CopyDescriptorsSimple from a CPU-only
heap, a stale material table) copied the mirror's dead descriptor into
the destination's place in the shared heap and recorded it as naming
nothing, so no later destroy would ever null it: a shader sampling it
touches unmapped memory, the fault resource_gone exists to prevent.

A claimed index is now recorded as GONE instead of 0. names_of hands
that to publish_range, which writes the null view of its kind over a
GONE source's copy in the shared heap and records the destination as
GONE too, so a copy of that copy is nulled the same way. The check is
made where the copy is published, under SLOT_WRITES, and nothing is
written into the title's mirror, so a view the title makes in that slot
meanwhile is not overwritten. The lock order at SLOT_WRITES is kept:
the null views' source (GLOBAL) is taken before SLOT_WRITES, as in
resource_gone.

The new WARP test (in a child process, the shared heap being the
process's) makes an SRV of a texture in a CPU-only console heap, ends
the texture, copies the slot into a shader-visible heap and again from
there: the shared descriptors of both copies must be the null view and
named GONE. Without the publish_range change the first copy holds the
texture's view.

D3D12.X: no giant driver compile of a pipeline nobody has used yet

The lane of giant driver compiles (4 MiB of DXIL or more) has one slot,
for wanted builds too (the hard cap from upstream), and the backlog
builds pipelines ahead of their first use on its lowest-priority workers.
Together a giant build ahead could take the free slot, and a giant build
a bind waits for then stood behind it for that whole compile (minutes),
because a slot is never given back before the compile ends.

A build ahead of its pipeline's first use now takes no slot in that lane:
it waits there, holding none, until its pipeline is used (a bind wants it
and it takes the wanted slot, or a bind gave up on it and it waits like
any unwanted build). It does not spin: it sleeps on the lane's condvar
with the same 50 ms re-check as every waiter. So that a pipeline the title
never uses cannot hold up the backlog, the waiting build's backlog worker
gives back the lane of new compute pipelines and a new worker starts in
its place (pso_async::build_parks); the waiting thread ends after its
build. The BIG lane is unchanged: it keeps a wanted slot free beside the
one an unwanted build can take.

D3D12.X: image-only compute builds go to the backlog, not the bind queue

With XCL_PSO_IMAGE_SKIP=1 a bind does not wait for a big compute program
that writes only images; resolve_spared sent its build to the normal
worker queue. Those builds are unwanted, so each one, after translation
and DXC, waits in big_compile_turn for the single unwanted slot of huge
driver compiles. A world start binds hundreds of such programs: with more
of them queued than there are workers, every worker sat in that wait, and
with a wait budget (XCL_CS_PSO_WAIT_MS or XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS) a build a bind
waits for, which only the workers build then, stood in the queue behind
them until the bind's budget ran out.

Their builds now go to the build-ahead backlog, in the lane of new compute
pipelines (Backlog::spared): handed out one at a time with that lane,
before its pipelines, and also short of commit or past XCL_PSO_AHEAD,
since these pipelines are used. The normal workers stay free for builds a
bind waits for. Without the backlog (XCL_PSO_PRELOAD=0) the build goes to
the normal workers as before, and with XCL_PSO_IMAGE_SKIP unset no
pipeline is spared, so nothing changes.

D3D12.X: a partial upload re-arms the stream recheck without a baseline

Since only a whole upload seeds the stream recheck baseline, a partial
upload of an unwatched texture that has no recheck entry (it retired
after its last milestone, was pruned while its range was watched, or
was never seeded) did nothing. Writes to its unwatched pages after that
upload went unnoticed until something else made the texture pending.
Before, the partial upload re-created the entry, with a fingerprint of
memory the GPU never got.

Such a partial upload now inserts an entry without a baseline
(last_fp: None). Its first milestone always queues the texture, and the
whole upload that follows sets the real baseline. An existing entry is
still left alone by a partial upload, so its baseline and schedule stay
those of the last whole upload.

The cost is at most one extra whole upload per partial upload of a
texture without an entry, four frames later.

- once a bind waits for the giant one (resolve_wait_for), it goes

- the waiting thread then ends, leaving as many backlog workers as

- while another new compute build holds the lane, the end of the giant

D3D12.X: the driver watch logs a long call and holds lists only for a stop

The watch held every later submit of every thread once an
ExecuteCommandLists or Present had not returned for XCL_GPU_STALL_MS,
with no time limit. A call that only waits for GPU progress which
depends on a submit the gate then parks (a cross-queue fence, a Write64
wait bridged to a queue Wait) never returns, so a slow moment became a
permanent stop. The stop file was read on the same thread, after the
device poll: had GetDeviceRemovedReason not returned in a driver error,
the stop would never have been taken and the process would have been
killed from outside with GPU work in flight.

- A long call is logged when it passes the limit (with the ring), every
  5 s while it lasts, and when it returns, with the real length of the
  stall (its start is kept on its own; the old line computed it from
  the time last said, which every 5 s overwrote). The decision is a pure
  step function (watch_step) with tests, among them a 13 s stall.
- Command lists are held only while a stop for a driver error is being
  handled (HOLD, set by the stop file's fault path). The wait takes the
  flag, and returns at once on a thread that is itself inside a timed
  call (it would wait on itself).
- The stop file is read on its own thread (xcl-stop-file), also with
  XCL_GPU_WATCH=0, which calls nothing in the driver before the title
  ends. It is read as bytes: a file that is still empty is ignored (10
  polls in a row: end), a UTF-8 BOM is stripped, UTF-16 LE is decoded.
  On a fault it waits 12 s for the watch thread's device poll, and
  says when that poll itself has not returned (a heartbeat).
- The 65th thread that asks for a slot is logged once.

Three corrections to the forgotten-ask count of c9fe50e (sparse.rs):

- take_asks counted every ask it left out (no pair for the tile, a tile
  with its own memory, no window index). An address a title binds at
  every draw is left out at every submit: every thread's memory of its
  asks was emptied at every submit, the threads asked again and the next
  submit counted again, a steady loop that defeated the memory. That
  branch removes the tile from the asked set uncounted again, as before
  c9fe50e; a pair made later already changes the views' generation.
- forget_mirrors took the tiles out of the asked set first and out of
  the queue after. An ask on another thread in between inserted the tile
  as new and queued it, and the queue's retain then deleted it: the tile
  stayed asked for, in no queue, with no count after it, and was never
  mapped (the GPU read zeros there). The queue goes first now: an ask in
  between finds the tile still asked for, or stays queued, and the count
  after it has the thread ask again.
- forget_mirrors_in dropped asks a submit had taken (their CPU view
  forgotten) and left them in the asked set: asked for again, they were
  not queued. Each ask it drops is forgotten (and counted) now.

Recompiler: a compute loop's passes shrink with the dispatch's size

A lane may run 65 536 loop passes before LOOP_GUARD ends its loops, so
that console code looping on a count XCL gave it wrong does not keep the
GPU busy for minutes. That bound is per lane: the work it allows grows
with the dispatch, and a large dispatch outlasts the 2 s Windows waits
before it removes the device.

WindNew:CS_AdvectFromParentStep (a542b07e605c8fd7, 4 x 4 x 4 threads) is
dispatched as 16 x 16 x 16 groups and loops while a counter differs from
a count in title memory. Run alone on an RTX 3060 Ti with synthetic
inputs, the translated program takes 1.0 ms with a count of 0, 6.7 ms
with 64, 25 ms with 256 – and with a count that never comes 111 ms when
the loop is ended after 256 passes and 485 ms after 1024 (0.47 ms a
pass), which is 31 s for 65 536. That is the dispatch left open when the
device was removed (#1452).

A compute dispatch whose group counts are known now passes its share of
2^28 loop passes for one group in a free io slot (IO_LOOP_BUDGET), and
in a compute program every entry of a loop has its own count of passes:
that share among the group's threads, between 1024 and 65 536 a lane.
Up to 4096 lanes nothing changes; at 16 x 16 x 16 groups of 64 threads
one entry of a loop ends after 1024 passes. The lane's budget of 65 536
for all its loops stays, so loops inside one another are not cut to one
loop's share: only a loop that runs away on its own is ended early. A
slot of 0 (an indirect dispatch, the test runner) leaves 65 536, and
programs without a loop, other stages and the direct translator emit
what they did.

Recompiler: find the loop directly around each loop of a direct CFG

The direct DXIL translator's compute programs are to count each entry of
a loop against the dispatch's share, as the HLSL path does since the
previous commit. An inner loop's count has to start afresh each time the
loop is entered, and the translator lowers blocks one by one with no
idea of which loop holds which: Cfg only knows the loop headers.

cfg::loop_parents gives, for each loop header of the (reducible) Cfg, the
header of the loop directly around it, or none. A loop is its header and
every block that reaches one of its back edges (an edge into the header
from a block at or after it in the reverse post-order) without passing
the header; the loop around it is the smallest other loop that holds its
header. Nothing calls it yet.

Recompiler: direct compute loops count each entry against the dispatch

The previous commits made the HLSL path's compute loops end an entry
after the dispatch's share of passes for a thread (IO_LOOP_BUDGET), so
that a large dispatch whose loop count never comes does not outlast the
time Windows gives the GPU before it resets the driver. Compute programs
run through the direct DXIL translator here, and it kept only the lane's
budget of 65 536 passes for all its loops, which a retail title's program
dispatched as 16 x 16 x 16 groups turns into about 31 s of GPU time.

The plain form of a compute program with a loop now loads the slot once
in the entry block and makes cap = slot == 0 ? 65 536 : clamp(slot /
threads per group, DISPATCH_LOOP_PASSES_MIN, 65 536), the HLSL path's
xcl_cap. Each loop header b has a variable VAR_LOOP_PASSES + b (1 << 30
and up: above the temporaries and the reload variables), set to cap at
the entry; a loop's head, before the lane's budget, leaves to the
program's end when its count is 0, else counts it down, and sets the
counts of the loops directly inside it (cfg::loop_parents) back to cap.
In a reducible CFG every path that enters a loop passes the head of the
loop around it, so that is a fresh count on every entry. A loop that
runs out ends the lane's program, where the HLSL path goes on after the
loop; both only end a loop that ran away. The lane's budget stays as it
was. Programs without a loop and every other entry emit what they did;
the compact form and the per-lane form keep the lane's budget alone.

D3D12.X: cap the scratch chained dispatches hold together

Every chained Dispatch of upstream's split programs creates its own committed
scratch buffer (DEFAULT heap, zero-filled), of groups x dwords_per_group x 4
bytes, and keeps it until its allocator is reset or released. dwords_per_group
is the stride (1 + the words of every value live across any cut) times the
group's threads, so a 16x16x16 grid of 32-thread groups takes stride x 512 KiB;
at stride 100 that is 50 MB for one dispatch, and the only limit was 4 GiB per
dispatch. Fifty such dispatches a frame with three frames in flight would hold
about 7.5 GB.

The bytes every not yet released chained dispatch holds are now counted
(SCRATCH_HELD: taken before the buffer is made, given back when it cannot be
made and when its Recording is dropped at the allocator's Reset or Release).
A dispatch that would take them past XCL_DIRECT_SPLIT_SCRATCH_MB (default
1024 MiB) runs the whole program instead, as one whose scratch could not be
made, with a log line (the first four, then powers of two). The periodic
"compute split" line also gives the MiB held. README: the variable.

Left as it was: one buffer per dispatch, zero-filled, made on the title's
thread. Keeping one buffer per recording, grown to the largest size asked,
needs a key per recording (two recordings on one allocator may run at once)
and is a larger change.

what fits, refuses what would pass the cap without taking anything, takes
again what was given back, and does not overflow).

Recompiler: loads through s_getpc_b64 read the constant data after the program

Console programs keep constant tables after s_endpgm and read them
PC-relative (s_getpc_b64 + s_load_dword* / global_load_dword*). The
translation gave s_getpc_b64 the program offset with high dword 0, so in
a title these loads read memory window 0 at a low offset: zeros. 676 of
the 26503 shader records of a retail title use this, among them all
postfx_aces LUT bakes, whose 64-cube output LUT came out as one constant
texel, so the presented image was flat.

The data blocks after the program (xbox::Fssm::rodata, the new
Options::rodata) now go with the translation:

- HLSL: emit.rs embeds them as `static const uint xcl_rodata[]`, and
  s_load and FLAT / GLOBAL dword loads go through xcl_gload*, which take
  the dwords at a code address inside a block from the table. With
  several memory windows s_getpc_b64's high dword is CODE_ADDRESS_HI
  (0xC0DE, above any user-space address), so a code address is told from
  the title's memory at the same low dword; with one window it is the
  program's offset as before.
- Direct DXIL: the same, as an internal constant array of the module
  (Lw::rodata_loads in lower_window.rs); with windows s_buffer_load reads
  it too. kernel::translate_entry_rodata carries the data. The per-lane
  form (XCL_PER_LANE) has no table and leaves such programs to the
  per-instruction form. TRANSLATOR_VERSION 9 -> 10.
- pso.rs passes the data on the compute, VS / PS and mesh paths (HLSL
  and direct), and `xcl shaders` (precompile, direct sweep) does too.

Not covered: byte / short global loads, MUBUF buffer_load, the legacy
GS path and the per-lane form still read memory at such addresses.

The console runs up to 2^32 - 1 thread groups a dimension; D3D12 takes
65 535, and past that a dispatch is undefined. On an NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti a
retail game's world loading hung the GPU (DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG,
0x887A0006) about 100 s in, every run: the only unfinished work was an

markers of #1323), and its arguments, written by an earlier dispatch, were

word (IO_GROUP_LIMIT, in the trap-temp range like IO_UMA_BASE_HI; 0 when
not folded), and every translated compute program takes

cannot be folded (two dimensions past the limit) is clamped and logged.

Shaders: fall back to the process heap when a private DXC heap fails

A worker's compiler was made through DxcCreateInstance2 with a private
heap, and only E_INVALIDARG fell back to plain DxcCreateInstance. Any
other HRESULT (E_NOINTERFACE, REGDB_E_CLASSNOTREG from a different DXC
build), S_OK without an object, or a HeapCreate failure under commit
pressure failed the compile, and every later job on that worker failed
the same way, where the shared process heap had compiled it. Now any
failure of the private path warns once with the reason and makes the
compiler on the process heap; only a failure there too is an error.

The private heap is also no longer destroyed with its allocator. Before
the private heaps all DXC memory came from one heap, so a block DXC
keeps past its compiler (lazily made global state, freed later through
another compiler) could not dangle. With HeapDestroy on the last
release it would, for a thread that exits (the tests' scoped threads do).
Pool workers never exit, so in the runtime the heaps already lived until
the process ends; this costs nothing there.

Tested (release, software adapter): new tests show the fallback for
three failing DxcCreateInstance2 results, that a block outlives its
allocator, and that a private-heap compiler gives byte-identical DXIL
to a process-heap compiler for the same pixel shader. Whole library
suite run on this commit.

kernelx: an address keeps the page the title mapped there last

The queue's CopyPageMappingsBatchX names pool addresses, and on the
console a physical page stays mapped at every address the title mapped
it at. XCL keeps a page's bytes in one place: Away::at holds an address
only while the bytes are kept there, and when the title maps the same
page at a second address XCL moves the bytes and move_away drops the
first address - which is the pool address the method names. So the
method could not tell which page a pool address holds.

Away gains title: address -> the page the title mapped there last.
map_pages clears an address's entry first and writes it only once the
page is in place (at home, after a move, at the lazy insert, at the
final insert); a failed map leaves none. FreeTitlePhysicalPages drops
the entries of the freed pages with one retain (page numbers are never
handed out again); the release of a sparse, view-window or graphics
reservation forgets the entries inside it. Bookkeeping only: nothing
reads it yet, no behaviour change.

needs to know, from the view and the DSV, which buffer they name and in
which PC state it was made. This commit only keeps that, behind

registered and every hook stops at one atomic load.

  CreatePlacedResource and its memory of its own (0 after its retry). A
  single-sample 2D buffer with flags 6 and PC format 19/39/44/53 is kept;
  objects at one title address and shape share a Cell (on the PC they
  share texels), a buffer without a title address is a Cell of its own;
- note_dsv at CreateDepthStencilView, and DSV descriptor copies
  (CopyDescriptorsSimple, CopyDescriptors range by range) followed: the

the PC UAV, the published name, the companion SRV and the T# (GFX10
format 5, uint) come by the ordinary path of a texture with unordered
access. A UAV of the depth plane, of a buffer XCL did not see created,
or with the switch off stays a null view, counted with its reason.

kernelx: a GPU-view page follows its physical page where it is kept

The record of the queue's page-mapping method keeps, for each GPU-view
page it named, where XCL keeps the shown physical page's bytes. XCL
moves those bytes whenever the title maps the page at another address
or unmaps it (one place per page), so the place has to follow, on the
moving thread and before the memory the page leaves can go: otherwise a
reader of the record (and, later, a tile linked to the place) reads an
address that was decommitted under it.

mirrors::page_at(page, at, tile) moves the place of every GPU-view page
that shows the physical page (the reverse index by_page), with by_at
and the 16 MiB block counts; its call and its place in the log stay - a
move is no change of what the page shows - unless the page gets its
first place or loses it (its bytes appear or go). One atomic load while
nothing is recorded, and a read-locked lookup before the write lock.
mirrors::page_freed(page): the pages that showed a freed page show
nothing (a change). kernelx::page_placed calls page_at with the tile
flag (a home, unified memory or a graphics reservation) and notes a
moved page as a known write at its new address
(title_textures::note_known_write): a CPU write made just before the
move went with the page. Called, with AWAY held: in move_away after the
copy and before release_at, in unmap_away in both branches (before the
release), in map_pages at the lazy insert, after the copy from home
(before move_home_away can give the home back) and in the zero branch;
FreeTitlePhysicalPages calls page_freed for every page of the call.
Still not reached by the runtime: the record stays empty until the
queue method is turned on.

kernelx: the changed pages of a GPU view, and the views a write reaches

What the textures need from the record of the queue's page-mapping
method, ahead of their use: which GPU-view pages show something else
now, and which GPU-view pages a CPU write reaches.

mirrors::changes_since(seen, lo, hi, most) walks the record's log from
a reader's cursor: each GPU-view page in [lo, hi) whose content changed

unmapped GPU-view page gets nothing from the CPU view under it. One

D3D12.X: the tiles of a GPU view show the pages mapped into them

The record of the queue's page-mapping method (kernelx::mirrors) says
what each GPU-view page shows; the tiles of the view windows still
showed the CPU view at the same offset, so a streamed page the title
mapped into its GPU view never reached the GPU there.

A tile now shows what the record says (tile_shows, behind
mirror_source_tile and cpu_of): the CPU view's tile for a page never
named, the place a mapped page is kept when a tile may show it there,
nothing for an unmapped page, one with no page or one kept where
kernelx does not see the memory go. cpu_of gives the place whatever its
tile flag (the CPU reads and writes any). With an empty record every

apply_batches for the pages whose entry changed, page_freed, place_gone,
and page_placed for a page that gets or loses its place); it queues the
tiles that were asked for (REMAPS, a lock of its own, no state's lock).
The next submit links them again (remap_mirrors, at most 4096, after the
finished copies back land and before map_mirrors): video memory over
the new place is cleared and filled from its committed pages ahead of
the older asks; a tile that shows nothing gives its video memory back
and stays asked for. A placed buffer's tile keeps its pool tile, cleared,
over no_source (64 KiB of XCL's own, reserved, never committed), because
the buffer maps its tiles once. take_asks leaves a tile that shows
nothing asked for (a later mapping finds it); buffer_tiles links one
over no_source. unlink_kept and park, the halves of unlink_mirror and
drop_mirror, keep the ask: forgetting it would empty every recording
thread's memory of its asks at every change. Still not reached by the
runtime: the record stays empty until the queue method is turned on.

D3D12.X: a tile of a GPU view follows its page when the page moves

XCL keeps a physical page's bytes in one place and moves them whenever
the title maps the page elsewhere or unmaps it; the record of the queue's
page mappings follows the page (mirrors::page_at), and the place it left
is decommitted or released right after. A tile linked over the old place
would then be given back and filled again at the new one, or, worse,
read memory that is going. A move is no remap: the bytes are the same.

sparse::moved(tiles, from, to, whole), called by kernelx::page_placed on
the moving thread with AWAY held and before the old place can go, takes
the state's lock only when a tile shows `from` (SOURCES), giving way to
submits. State::retarget moves the link of each tile linked over `from`:
with video memory and the page's 64 KiB copied (`whole`) the entry keeps
its pool tile, gen and sent hashes, and nothing is cleared or filled -
the known write kernelx notes at the new place brings its pages to the
next scan, which sends only what differs, and a copy back recorded
before the move lands at the new place. A page never used (not
committed at the new place) gives its video memory up and waits there
like any linked tile. A page that moves to a place no tile may show (plain
memory) is queued with remapped instead, and shows nothing from the next
submit; the old place is told to sparse when it goes. Counted in
page_tiles()[1]. Still not reached by the runtime while the record is
empty.

D3D12.X: a texture goes up again when a mapping under it changes

When the queue's page mappings put another page under a texture read
through its pages, nothing was written: no write watch fires for a
clean, already filled pool page that is newly mapped, so the texture
kept the bytes of the page that was there before.

recheck_gpu_view_sources now also reads the GPU-view pages whose
mapping changed (mirrors::changes_since, 512 a submit: one upload
batch; the rest at the next), with one atomic compare when nothing
changed. It does not go through GPU_VIEW_MAP_LOG: that bumps the
generation that empties every recording thread's ask cache, and its
log of 4096 entries overflows into a recheck of every texture. A
texture becomes paged when a page under it is first named (pending, as
on today's source changes). For a paged texture that is not pending
the changed pages' bytes are stale: texture_upload::stale joins them
into what goes up again, and the existing AGAIN path sends them with no
comparison; the page hashes come to what went up. A shadowed texture is
made pending instead.

The GPU's write of a texture is noted per PC list as it is recorded
(note_gpu_write gains the list) and stamped when the list is submitted
(Entry::written_call = mirrors::calls()). A mapping changed by a later
call clears gpu_written and sends its pages; one changed before the
submit leaves the texture the GPU's. A list submitted again is stamped
again; a reset list writes nothing more. Textures read again are
counted (rereads).

The release of a block of unified memory (the title's MEM_GRAPHICS
allocations) told sparse nothing while GPU views show mapped pages: it
called source_going with size 0, which source_part only answers for a
paired CPU view. Yet unified memory counts as memory whose release
kernelx sees (freeing_is_seen), so tiles are linked over pages kept
there, and physical pages can be mapped into such blocks. The record
kept the place and Away::title kept the mapping, so once the block was
handed out again the tiles and paged textures showed the new owner's

resolved to the old page.

the title's mappings in it, leaves the shown pages kept there without a
place (mirrors::place_gone), tells sparse of the whole block, and has
their tiles linked again – all before Uma::free hands the block back.

address space was given back: a submit in between could link a tile
over the released range, and one reserved and committed again meanwhile
would fill it with unrelated bytes. The record is cleared before the
release now; sparse forgets the tiles over it and relinks the asked
ones after, as before.

forget_title_mappings removes the entries of each page of a range when
the range has fewer pages than there are entries, instead of a pass
over all of them: it now runs on every release of a block of unified
memory.

D3D12.X: a dispatch put off to the submit waits there until it is built

With XCL_PSO_WAIT_MS set, a Dispatch or dispatching ExecuteIndirect put
off to the submit (#2118) was recorded through resolve_wait, with the same
budget a bind has as the title records. A pipeline a bind had already
found late got the stand-in at once, one still building got it after the
budget, and the dispatch was counted as skipped and left out. Its segment
lies between the list's other work, so the list's Write64 labels, EOP
writes and fence signals still fired: the title saw the work as done
while its UAV outputs, counters and indirect argument buffers were never
written.

record_deferred now waits for the segment's compute pipeline
(pso_async::wait_for_submit) before it records the call, whether a bind
found it late or not. Without the budget this is the wait the submit
already made. With it, the submit leaves the build to the workers for
the budget first, as a bind does, so big compiles keep their turns on
the workers; one no worker has started by then is built on the
submitting thread, so a submit never waits for a free worker. One a
worker builds is waited for at most 30 s (SUBMIT_WAIT_MOST, the time a
retail title's watchdog lets its main thread stand still, #891):

D3D12.X: a depth plane twin is copied around the title's UAV transitions

A console title may make a UAV of a depth buffer and have compute passes
read and write its depth plane. The PC buffer has no unordered access, so
behind XCL_DEPTH_UAV_TWIN=1 the depth plane of a D32, D16 or D32S8 buffer
gets a twin (R32_TYPELESS, R16_TYPELESS) that must hold what the plane
holds while shaders use it, and give back what they wrote.

The title says when that is: it moves the buffer into UNORDERED_ACCESS
before its shaders use the UAV and out of it before the next depth test or
sampling, and each transition names the state it leaves and the one it
enters. So, in ResourceBarrier:

- The PC buffer cannot be in UNORDERED_ACCESS: where the title has it
  there it rests in COPY_SOURCE (depth_uav::PARK), on every list (also the
  console-shaped ones), from its creation on, so its states agree wherever
  the title moves it. An object the title made in UNORDERED_ACCESS keeps
  the title's states, and gets no copies.
- After a transition into UNORDERED_ACCESS on a DIRECT list, the depth
  plane is copied into the twin (the twin made then when there is none):
  what was drawn reaches the shaders.
- Before a transition out of it, the twin is copied into the plane, which
  goes PARK -> COPY_DEST, and the title's transition goes on from there:
  what the shaders wrote reaches the next draw.
- A copy into the twin is not done while the two hold the same: after a
  copy on this recording with no transition to a state that writes the
  plane since (in_step, per list, cleared by Reset and KickoffX; a split
  segment starts without it). Record order is execution order only within
  one list, so nothing is carried across lists.
- A twin whose last way in was not copied (a compute list, a twin that
  could not be made) is not copied back: it does not hold the plane.
- A split transition is done whole at its end.

D3D12 rules relied on: copies of whole subresources between a depth
plane and a texture of the same format family (R32_TYPELESS and
R16_TYPELESS on both sides; plane 0 of R32G8X24_TYPELESS copies as
R32_TYPELESS); a depth-stencil resource may be in COPY_SOURCE / COPY_DEST;
the twin rests in UNORDERED_ACCESS and goes to COPY_* and back around each
copy. Copies only on DIRECT lists.

The UAV itself still names nothing here; the next commit makes it a view
of the twin.

D3D12.X: a UAV of a depth plane can be a view of its R32 or R16 twin

With XCL_DEPTH_UAV_TWIN=1 a UAV of the depth plane of a D32, D16 or D32S8
buffer was still a null view ("its depth plane has no twin yet"): on a
retail title 11 of them in the first seconds of its 3D world, so its
compute lighting read nothing and wrote nowhere. It is now a view of the
plane's twin, made at the first such UAV or transition into
UNORDERED_ACCESS, the way the stencil plane's UAV is a view of its R8
twin: the slot's UAV, companion SRV and T# name the twin.

The view keeps the title's dimension, mip and slices on plane 0; its
format is R32_FLOAT (D32, D32S8) or R16_UNORM (D16), the depth as a
shader reads it, unless the title asked for another class of that size
(R32_UINT, R16_UINT ...). A D24S8's depth plane stays a null view (no UAV
format reads it as the depth), as does that of a buffer made in
UNORDERED_ACCESS (its states stay the title's, the twin would never be
copied). The stencil plane goes as before.

D3D12.X: switches to keep, poison and count the GPU-view tiles

Shaders that read zeros where data should be (vertices of prepared meshes
collapsing to a point, tile light lists read as empty) may be reading tiles
of the memory windows with no video memory: never filled, given back, or
asked for at a submit that ran before their fill. Nothing told these apart.
Three switches do, all off unless set:

- XCL_VIEW_KEEP=1: a tile over a CPU view keeps its video memory once
  filled. Where it would go back (its CPU view decommitted, its view gone,
  its page remapped or moved) it stays mapped in `kept` and is taken back
  from there as a parked tile is. Tiles kept count against XCL_MIRROR_MB;
  at the cap tiles are refused as before (warned once).
- XCL_VIEW_POISON=1 (or =0x<pattern>): every tile of the windows without
  video memory is mapped onto one shared tile filled with 0x7fc0dead
  (REUSE_SINGLE_TILE), and an unmapped tile goes back to it instead of
  NULL; a buffer placed in a window starts on it too. The tile is filled
  again at most every 16 ms, as shaders may write there.
- XCL_VIEW_STATS=1 (on with either of the others): a line every 2 s of the
  tiles asked for, filled, given back and kept, how many submits after
  going a tile got video memory again (0-1, 2-8, 9-64, more) and the bytes
  filled again for those, and the submits that left asked tiles waiting
  for a later submit (the fill budget and ask limit of a submit).

Which windows a pipeline's shaders reach is not known (the window comes
from each address at run time), so submits are not matched to the
windows their lists read.

Tests: the switches' pattern, the keep decision, the buckets and the line;
a kept tile stays mapped over a submit and comes back with its count; a
tile without video memory reads the pattern, filled reads its data, given
back reads the pattern again (on the software adapter).

D3D12.X: record the graphics pipelines a run uses with their state

The shader preparation before a title starts builds the compute pipelines
earlier runs used, but no graphics pipeline: what is kept between runs is
not enough to make one again. used-pipelines.txt holds only the key of a
pipeline's shader set, and the driver cache holds blobs named after the
translated DXIL and the description's hash. A retail title then builds
~6 000 graphics pipelines in its first minutes, with thousands of
stand-ins that draw nothing meanwhile.

A lazy graphics pipeline's description is now written down at its first
use in a run (pso_async::on_first_use, told once, as used::note is):
every field of the description but its pointers, its input layout, and
the keys of its console shaders, ~200 bytes, under the key
used-pipelines.txt has. The entry is made when the pipeline is (no
shader copy is kept for it after its build) and written by a thread of
its own, each description once, to used-graphics-pipelines.bin beside
the DXIL cache (gfx_records: the format is in the module's comment). The
file is versioned (another version reads as none and is started again),
an entry cut short or damaged ends it, and it stops at XCL_GFX_RECORDS_MB
(64) with a line in the log. No shader code is kept: the preparation
finds the shaders in the title's shader files by key, as it does for
used-shaders.txt.

Mesh pipeline streams are not recorded.

xcl run: build the graphics pipelines earlier runs used before the title

After the compute pass, the shader preparation now reads the graphics
pipeline records of earlier runs (used-graphics-pipelines.bin), finds
their console shaders in the title's shader files by key, and builds each
pipeline in worker processes, the way the title's background build makes
it (real::prepare_graphics calls translated_graphics_pso, as
build_graphics does): the translation, DXC and driver blob caches on disk
then hold exactly what the title asks for, and the title makes these
pipelines from the kept blob in milliseconds instead of compiling them
while it draws stand-ins.

Worker processes, as for the compute pipelines: the driver builds about
two pipelines at a time for one process, and a driver that ends a worker
ends no title. Nothing of the title's device is needed: a translated
pipeline gets XCL's root signature, and what else its build reads of the
process is the title's memory windows (given with --windows, no memory
reserved: uma::leave_out, pso::set_title_windows) and the adapter
(XCL_ADAPTER from the title's setting). Each worker gets a file of its
part with the shaders it needs (gfx_records' format) in the temporary
folder, removed after.

The title did not keep the blob of most graphics pipelines: none of under
16 KB of DXIL and none built in under 250 ms (XCL_PSO_DISK_CACHE_MIN_MS),
so most were compiled again in every run. A preparation worker keeps
every blob, on disk only. The blob's file name is made of the
description's state, the DXIL, the adapter and driver and the window
count, no address, so the title's lookup finds the worker's file.

The screen shows "Building graphics pipelines" with its own count, the
5 s line counts graphics pipelines, a failure is logged and skipped and
the title starts regardless. XCL_PREPARE=0 skips it with the rest,
XCL_PREPARE_GRAPHICS=0 skips this pass only.

Textures no longer wait for remappings of other title memory

Reads of title memory in place (texture refreshes at submission, rectangle
vertices) and the runtime's changes of its mapping (XMemMapPhysicalPages,
its scatter form, map_alias) shared one lock over all of title memory.
While the world streams in the title changes mappings 650-1,100 times a
frame, many a page at a time, so every refresh waited for changes anywhere
and every change for the refresh under way.

Now a read holds the bytes it reads and a change the bytes whose mapping it
changes (the range, and the whole of the views unmap takes away and maps
again); they wait for each other only where those meet. A change waiting
for a read keeps new reads of its bytes out, as the lock's writers did.
VICTORY_MAPPING_RANGES=0 holds all of title memory, as before. A new frame
line gives the changes per frame, the time they waited for reads in place
and the time they were under way.

Shaders: lower v_ldexp_f32, v_frexp_mant_f32 and v_frexp_exp_i32_f32

v_ldexp_f32: DXIL has no ldexp, so x is multiplied by three powers of two
that are each a normal float (q, q and e - 2q for q = e / 3). The exponent
is clamped to [-375, 378] first: past that any finite nonzero x is already
at zero or infinity, and inside it each factor's exponent stays in
[-126, 127]. Zeros, infinities and NaN pass through the multiplies
unchanged.

v_frexp_mant_f32 and v_frexp_exp_i32_f32 work on the bits, so denormals
are normalized whatever the host's float mode: the significand keeps the
sign with a magnitude in [0.5, 1), and x = significand * 2^exponent. Zero,
infinity and NaN return themselves and exponent 0.

All three were refused as unsupported before ("v_ldexp_f32 is not
supported"), which drops any draw or dispatch whose shader uses them.

Shaders: first-lane reads alike in a console wave need no exchange on 32-lane hosts

A console wave of 64 lanes runs on a 32-lane host (NVIDIA) as two host
waves, and a v_readfirstlane must then take the console's first lane
from the other half through LDS and group barriers, which only fit in
blocks every lane runs. Two compute programs of the world, a group-wide
prefix sum over 512 threads, were refused that way ("a first-lane read
where not every lane runs"): their loop over the waves before their own
reads the running sum with v_readfirstlane where only some waves run.

That sum, and the loop's lanes, are the same in all 64 lanes of a
console wave: made of scalars, of an LDS read at a scalar address after
the last LDS write and a group barrier, and of the console wave's number
(thread id >> 6). Such a read gives each host wave the console's answer
among its own lanes.

emit::coherent finds what the two host waves of a console wave hold
alike: values every lane of a console wave holds alike (VALU results of
such values, scalars and masks whose lane bits are alike, thread id bits
from 6 up where a row holds whole console waves, LDS reads at such
addresses where no instruction writes LDS past a barrier every lane
runs), and blocks and guarded instructions the lanes of a console wave
run all together or not at all. It is a greatest fixpoint, so values
carried around loops are judged by the whole loop. Lane-crossing
operations (v_mbcnt, DPP, lane reads and writes, permutes, swizzles,
interpolation, ds_read_addtid) are never alike. The lowering asks it at
a first-lane read; the same questions are there for the branches the
wave takes together and the lane masks read as data, next.

Tests: a group-wide prefix of the same shape (written for the test, 4
console waves) lowers for a 32-lane host, and is still refused when its
loop goes by thread id >> 5 (which differs between the halves) or when a
row of the group holds only half a console wave; it decodes as written,
instruction by instruction.
A Windows test validates it and runs it on a GPU of 32-lane waves,
checking every thread's sum. Type-checked and clippy-clean for
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (all features).

GPU: a submission's texture checks run several at a time (VICTORY_WIDE_TEXTURES=1)

While the world streams in, a submission checks hundreds of textures one
after another on the submitting thread: each is read, hashed whole and,
when it changed, detiled into its staging buffer. With the switch the
checks that come due in a batch are queued (Batch::textures_due) and run
at its next flush, before a step that writes title memory and before the
lists run, so their order against those steps is unchanged, on the
threads kept for the snapshots (shadow::wide_run). Each check reads its
texture's title memory and writes its own staging buffer and notes under
its own lock, and a texture is queued once per batch (texture_due), so no
two threads check the same texture. The frame line's "textures" counts
the time it took, not the threads' sum.

Ti, 8dd30ab, same binary, one launch each):

  both                           frame   ~518 ms, textures  ~16 ms

GPU: heap buffer pass looks only at marked slots; time split and visit counts in the fps line

The pass for shaders that pick buffers by index looked again at every
buffer view of the heap (81,000 in the world) every 16 passes and rebuilt
every copy's span from all views every pass. Now (heap_pass.rs) a slot is
looked at again when its view was written, its view table entry was freed
(descriptor::forget, which leaves the record as it was), its record in
title memory differs from the one last seen (a 12-byte compare), or it
found no host copy (every 16 passes); all slots every 256 passes as a

went. VICTORY_HEAP_PASS_FULL=1 brings back the old pass for A/B.

quickly; here every request is inflated and unpacked by a worker of ours

Shaders, GPU: halves moved through a 16-bit buffer view keep their bits

The title keeps half floats, and indices beside them, in buffers it views
as R16G16B16A16_UINT and R16_UINT, and its programs move them with
buffer_load_format_d16_* and buffer_store_format_d16_*: on the console
each channel's 16 bits go as they are, whatever kind the view's format
is. The DXIL moved them by way of 32-bit floats (load as float,
legacyF32ToF16; legacyF16ToF32, store as float), which only a float view
carries. Through the integer view every value read came out 0.

The network that drives the faces (compute_graph_ops, about 2,650
dispatches a frame, then ped_standard_head_cs) works in such buffers: its
24 MB of tensors and its output were all zeros for whole runs, and no
character's mouth moved.

- victory-shader: such an access through a view of a table moves the 16
  bits as unsigned integers (bufferLoad.i32, bufferStore.i32), and
  HostShader::half_views names the table descriptors it is done through.
- victory-gpu: a table with a 16-bit float or signed buffer view at one
  of those places is made afresh for the draw, with that view in the
  unsigned format of the same layout (descriptor::host::half_view). The
  title's own slot keeps the title's format for other programs.

shortcut: through a view of wider, normalised or signed 8-bit channels,
whose values the console converts to and from halves, the integers are
read and written unconverted (logged once, with the format; the title's
are 16-bit unsigned). Views reached another way than through a table
keep the float path.

GPU: a slot's texture gets its host copy before the heap's slots are locked

HostHeap::mirror held the heap's lock on its slots while `make` made the
host copy of the texture a view shows: a call into the graphics kernel,
a quarter of a millisecond to milliseconds. The pass over textures picked
by index makes hundreds of those a frame while the world streams in, and
every other recording thread that mirrored a slot of the same heap stood
waiting for the lock. The sampling profiler, in a cutscene's first
seconds on an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (25 November): 450 ms a frame of the
recording threads waiting in HostHeap::mirror, 12 of 38 s of the pass in
host_texture_as.

For a slot made for a draw that is not made from this view yet, the
texture's host copy (or the placed texture's resource and its host copy)
is made first, with the lock not held; `make` then finds it. The view is
read from the title's slot before the lock, as it was right after it.

GPU: a placed texture found mapped is not asked about again page by page

After the pass over textures picked by index stages a texture, it asked
whether all of the texture's memory is there (texture::staged): a look
at the working set for every page, and a one-byte read through the
kernel for every page the process has not touched, which is every page
of a texture just streamed in. For a placed texture the pass had just
counted the mapped bytes block by block (mapped_bytes) and found all of
them. In a cutscene's first seconds on an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU the second
look was 8.4 of the pass's 38 s (the sampling profiler, 25 November),
on the recording thread that runs the pass.

A placed texture mapped_bytes found whole is taken as whole
(texture::staged_bytes gives its staged size without the look). Title
memory is mapped in 64 KiB pages, and a page mapped or unmapped later
makes the slot due again. Texture objects and partly mapped textures are
asked as before.

The card compare hashes a piece with a group of 64 threads: our passes on the card from about 35 to about 10 ms a frame

The compare of copies in the card's memory (`CARD_COMPARE`) gave each
64 KiB piece one thread, which walked it 16 bytes at a time, 4,096 loads
one after the other: a pass took the time of one piece however few pieces
it had, and the card ran next to nothing else meanwhile. The passes run
before every submission's lists (hashes after ranges are sent up, 300 to
450 a frame here) and after them (compares, about 100).

`CARD_COMPARE_WIDE` gives a piece a group: thread t hashes the 16-byte
steps t, t + 64, t + 128... (neighbouring threads read neighbouring
bytes) and the first thread folds the 64 lane hashes in lane order. It is
another hash, so a process uses one form for everything it stores and
compares: VICTORY_CARD_HASH_WIDE=0 keeps the thread a piece. A copy is
under 1 GiB, so a pass has at most 16,385 pieces, a group each, within
one dispatch.

Tests: the existing WARP test of the compare's modes runs both forms, and
a new one changes single bytes at offsets 0 to 65,535 of pieces of a copy
that does not start on a piece boundary, from a span that does not start
at piece 0: each change is flagged in its piece alone, in both forms.

GPU: the write-watch journal is let go while the kernel is asked

`watch::writes` held the journal's lock for its GetWriteWatch call and
for the guards' walk when that failed. The copies a submission brings up
to date on several threads (VICTORY_WIDE_REFRESH=1) and the texture
refreshes each ask about their own range, and they stood in line for the
lock, one asking at a time: the sampling profiler on an RTX 4060 Laptop
GPU (25 November, normal play) found our submitting thread 48 ms a frame
waiting for it, of a 268 ms frame, and the wide workers on a processor 8 %
of the time.

The asking now runs with the lock let go, into a buffer of the thread's
own. Its range is noted busy in the journal meanwhile: a `writes` or
`asked` whose pages overlap it, and every asking ahead (`ask_ahead`,
`ask_once`), waits until its pages are in the journal, so nothing finds
pages reset by the kernel and not noted yet. Ranges that do not overlap
are asked at the same time. The pages found get their asking's number
when the lock is taken again; a number can only be later than before,
which copies a page again, never misses one.

GPU: an async present waits for the one before it instead of running the line

With VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT=1, a present that found the present before it
still in a queue's line ran the old way: the title's thread ran the
queues' lines itself, holding the releaser's lock, while our submitting
thread stood waiting for that lock, and the next frame began with an
empty line. So only every other frame went behind: the frame log shows
pairs of a 3 ms and a 290 ms frame, and the sampling profiler (RTX 4060
Laptop GPU, 25 November) our thread 46 ms a frame waiting for the
releaser's lock and 27 ms with nothing to do.

The title's present now waits until our thread has shown the frame
before (one frame ahead at most, as before), then goes behind as well.
The wait is VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT_WAIT_MS (250 by default; 0: as
before); past it, a line that stands at a fence or memory value only the
title would meet runs the old way, which forces it. The 512-presents
line says how many waited in vain.

Game clock: the title's frames held to a steady step at low frame rates

The title times its frames with QueryPerformanceCounter and moves the
world by what it measured. At 3-4 fps that is 250-300 ms a step: a boat
at speed passes through a shore between two steps, the people on it are
thrown off, and a frame of steering is a quarter of a second.

With VICTORY_GAME_STEP_MS=33 the title's counter (served by the HLE for
api-ms-win-core-profile) runs slower while frames are slow, so a frame
counts about 33 ms for the title: the game runs slower than real time
instead of in jumps. The rate is set at each present from the frames
before it; the counter stays continuous and never goes back, a stall
still moves it, and the rate never drops below 1/32. Off by default; the
log says every five seconds how fast the game runs against real time.

play.ps1 -Steady sets it (-Step <ms> for another step).

xtask: find the repository root at run time

workspace_root() used env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"), a macro that bakes the
build machine's path into the binary at compile time. When the repository
moves to a different drive letter, cargo xtask policy --staged (the
pre-commit hook) fails with "The directory name is invalid" because the
embedded path no longer exists.

Find the root at run time instead:
1. git rev-parse --show-toplevel -- fast, correct in any worktree.
2. Walk up from std::env::current_dir() looking for .victory-root.
3. Fall back to CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR/.. for edge cases.

in the returned path, which the old compile-time approach would fail on a
moved repo.

Shaders: v_cvt_f32_f64

Two compute programs of the world stopped on it ("v_cvt_f32_f64 is
not supported"), and their dispatches were dropped. The conversion is
worked out on the double's bits in 64-bit integers, so the host needs no
double-precision support: round to nearest even, denormal results kept,
f64 denormals to zeros of their sign, NaNs quiet with their sign, past
the largest f32 infinity. Float inline constants are read as f64 values,
a literal as the high dword; abs and neg act on the sign bit.

Shaders: v_fma_mixlo/mixhi over an f16 first interpolation half keeps zero

A v_fma_mixlo_f16 into the VGPR of an f16 interpolation's first half

the failure reached the colour export and refused the whole program,
reported as "the first half of an interpolation". Nothing reads the kept
high half. write_half and low_half already keep zero for an old value

Textures no longer wait for remappings of other title memory

Reads of title memory in place (texture refreshes at submission, rectangle
vertices) and the runtime's changes of its mapping (XMemMapPhysicalPages,
its scatter form, map_alias) shared one lock over all of title memory.
While the world streams in the title changes mappings 650-1,100 times a
frame, many a page at a time, so every refresh waited for changes anywhere
and every change for the refresh under way.

Now a read holds the bytes it reads and a change the bytes whose mapping it
changes (the range, and the whole of the views unmap takes away and maps
again); they wait for each other only where those meet. A change waiting
for a read keeps new reads of its bytes out, as the lock's writers did.
VICTORY_MAPPING_RANGES=0 holds all of title memory, as before. A new frame
line gives the changes per frame, the time they waited for reads in place
and the time they were under way.

Paired runs on one exe (1684989 + this change) with a warm shader cache,
RTX 5070 Ti, 8 min each, medians over the world; A with
VICTORY_MAPPING_RANGES=0, B without:
- frame 801 -> 486 ms (mean 1,099 -> 524, p90 2,199 -> 670)
- textures 371 -> 47 ms, of them waiting for title memory to hold still
  203 -> 0 ms (mean 389 -> 0.6)
- texture bytes read 233 -> 288 MB/s: nothing is left out
- the runtime's changes waiting for reads 37 -> 0 ms a frame
- GPU 150 -> 135 ms, copies 44 -> 45, copy back 79 -> 72; drops 375 -> 363
- no device removal in either; slow submissions 4 and 5
- frames: the same lit opening scenes, B further into them in the time
For comparison, VICTORY_TEXTURE_NO_WAIT=1 on 1684989 (pair 768 -> 530 ms)
reads 91 MB/s against 228 and leaves ~61 refreshes a frame for later.

GPU: no blending on integer render targets

The host refuses a pipeline that enables blending on a target whose
format holds integers; the console writes such targets unblended
whatever the blend state says. One mesh pipeline of the world was
refused that way ("The parameter is incorrect"; the debug layer: "The
render target format at slot 2 is (R8_UINT). this format does not support
blending"), and its draws were dropped.

Once a pipeline stream is read, blending and logic operations are turned
off on its integer targets. A blend state that is not independent gives
every target the first one's settings, so it is made independent first,
with those settings on every target.

Shaders: lower v_ldexp_f32, v_frexp_mant_f32 and v_frexp_exp_i32_f32

v_ldexp_f32: DXIL has no ldexp, so x is multiplied by three powers of two
that are each a normal float (q, q and e - 2q for q = e / 3). The exponent
is clamped to [-375, 378] first: past that any finite nonzero x is already
at zero or infinity, and inside it each factor's exponent stays in
[-126, 127]. Zeros, infinities and NaN pass through the multiplies
unchanged.

v_frexp_mant_f32 and v_frexp_exp_i32_f32 work on the bits, so denormals
are normalized whatever the host's float mode: the significand keeps the
sign with a magnitude in [0.5, 1), and x = significand * 2^exponent. Zero,
infinity and NaN return themselves and exponent 0.

All three were refused as unsupported before ("v_ldexp_f32 is not
supported"), which drops any draw or dispatch whose shader uses them.

Tests: emit::tests::ldexp_and_frexp_translate (any OS) checks that the
VOP1/VOP3 forms, with abs and neg, translate. On Windows (host GPU and
WARP), valu_tests::v_frexp_mant_and_exp_f32_match_rdna2 covers zeros,
infinities, NaNs, both ends of the normal range and denormals, and
valu_tests::v_ldexp_f32_scales_by_any_exponent covers exponents a single
factor cannot hold, i32::MIN and i32::MAX, overflow, underflow and the
special values (normal inputs and results only, so the host's denormal
mode cannot change them).

Textures picked by index are looked at again after their upload (characters' skin and hair without colour in most launches)

A texture a shader picks by index was uploaded once, when the title wrote
its view, and again only if the view was rewritten or the runtime told of
a remap. The title often fills the texture's memory only afterwards (its
streaming reads land later), so the host copy kept what the memory held at
the first look for the rest of the run: zeros. Which textures lost that
race changed from launch to launch; the main character's face came out
black and her hair pale in about three launches of four.

Now a texture uploaded whole is looked at again after 4, 12, 40, 120 and
400 frames (a fingerprint of 48 KiB of its memory); a changed one is
uploaded again and the looks start over. One test launch re-uploaded more
than 6,000 textures this way. VICTORY_HEAP_RECHECK=0 turns it off.

Known gap: the fingerprint samples the start, middle and end of the
memory, so a texture whose other parts arrive later is still missed.

Shaders: first-lane reads alike in a console wave need no exchange on 32-lane hosts

A console wave of 64 lanes runs on a 32-lane host (NVIDIA) as two host
waves, and a v_readfirstlane must then take the console's first lane
from the other half through LDS and group barriers, which only fit in
blocks every lane runs. Two compute programs of the world, a group-wide
prefix sum over 512 threads, were refused that way ("a first-lane read
where not every lane runs"): their loop over the waves before their own
reads the running sum with v_readfirstlane where only some waves run.

That sum, and the loop's lanes, are the same in all 64 lanes of a
console wave: made of scalars, of an LDS read at a scalar address after
the last LDS write and a group barrier, and of the console wave's number
(thread id >> 6). Such a read gives each host wave the console's answer
among its own lanes.

emit::coherent finds what the two host waves of a console wave hold
alike: values every lane of a console wave holds alike (VALU results of
such values, scalars and masks whose lane bits are alike, thread id bits
from 6 up where a row holds whole console waves, LDS reads at such
addresses where no instruction writes LDS past a barrier every lane
runs), and blocks and guarded instructions the lanes of a console wave
run all together or not at all. It is a greatest fixpoint, so values
carried around loops are judged by the whole loop. Lane-crossing
operations (v_mbcnt, DPP, lane reads and writes, permutes, swizzles,
interpolation, ds_read_addtid) are never alike. The lowering asks it at
a first-lane read; the same questions are there for the branches the
wave takes together and the lane masks read as data, next.

Tests: a group-wide prefix of the same shape (written for the test, 4
console waves) lowers for a 32-lane host, and is still refused when its
loop goes by thread id >> 5 (which differs between the halves) or when a
row of the group holds only half a console wave; it decodes as written,
instruction by instruction.
A Windows test validates it and runs it on a GPU of 32-lane waves,
checking every thread's sum. Type-checked and clippy-clean for
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (all features).

FidelityFX capability, FSR 4 (type 7); otherwise its own (type 6, as on a
Series X). FSR 4's output never reaches the screen under VIctory, so every
world frame was black with `--console series-s`, and holding its DLL back
makes the title divide by zero in the FSR 4 wrapper.

before it is mapped and gets a file name of its own.

adds more.

6.4 fps steady (about 73 ms on the GPU), against 4.7 to 4.8 fps on the
Series X profile.

GPU: a submission's texture checks run several at a time (VICTORY_WIDE_TEXTURES=1)

While the world streams in, a submission checks hundreds of textures one
after another on the submitting thread: each is read, hashed whole and,
when it changed, detiled into its staging buffer. With the switch the
checks that come due in a batch are queued (Batch::textures_due) and run
at its next flush, before a step that writes title memory and before the
lists run, so their order against those steps is unchanged, on the
threads kept for the snapshots (shadow::wide_run). Each check reads its
texture's title memory and writes its own staging buffer and notes under
its own lock, and a texture is queued once per batch (texture_due), so no
two threads check the same texture. The frame line's "textures" counts
the time it took, not the threads' sum.

Measured on the opening cutscene and the first world minutes (RTX 3090
Ti, 8dd30ab, same binary, one launch each):

  default                        frame ~1,030 ms, textures ~330 ms
  VICTORY_WIDE_TEXTURES=1         frame   ~826 ms, textures ~120 ms
  VICTORY_TEXTURE_NO_WAIT=1       frame   ~654 ms, textures  ~44 ms
  both                           frame   ~518 ms, textures  ~16 ms

Steady state after streaming: 4.0-4.3 fps in all four.

GPU: heap buffer pass looks only at marked slots; time split and visit counts in the fps line

The pass for shaders that pick buffers by index looked again at every
buffer view of the heap (81,000 in the world) every 16 passes and rebuilt
every copy's span from all views every pass. Now (heap_pass.rs) a slot is
looked at again when its view was written, its view table entry was freed
(descriptor::forget, which leaves the record as it was), its record in
title memory differs from the one last seen (a 12-byte compare), or it
found no host copy (every 16 passes); all slots every 256 passes as a
safety net. A copy's span is worked out again only when one of its slots
went. VICTORY_HEAP_PASS_FULL=1 brings back the old pass for A/B.

The fps line now splits the pass's time: slots looked at, copies
refreshed, and the texture side (heap_textures, bounded at 250 ms a pass),

Shaders, GPU: halves moved through a 16-bit buffer view keep their bits

The title keeps half floats, and indices beside them, in buffers it views
as R16G16B16A16_UINT and R16_UINT, and its programs move them with
buffer_load_format_d16_* and buffer_store_format_d16_*: on the console
each channel's 16 bits go as they are, whatever kind the view's format
is. The DXIL moved them by way of 32-bit floats (load as float,
legacyF32ToF16; legacyF16ToF32, store as float), which only a float view
carries. Through the integer view every value read came out 0.

The network that drives the faces (compute_graph_ops, about 2,650
dispatches a frame, then ped_standard_head_cs) works in such buffers: its
24 MB of tensors and its output were all zeros for whole runs, and no
character's mouth moved.

- victory-shader: such an access through a view of a table moves the 16
  bits as unsigned integers (bufferLoad.i32, bufferStore.i32), and
  HostShader::half_views names the table descriptors it is done through.
- victory-gpu: a table with a 16-bit float or signed buffer view at one
  of those places is made afresh for the draw, with that view in the
  unsigned format of the same layout (descriptor::host::half_view). The
  title's own slot keeps the title's format for other programs.

shortcut: through a view of wider, normalised or signed 8-bit channels,
whose values the console converts to and from halves, the integers are
read and written unconverted (logged once, with the format; the title's
are 16-bit unsigned). Views reached another way than through a table
keep the float path.

HostHeap::mirror held the heap's lock on its slots while `make` made the
host copy of the texture a view shows: a call into the graphics kernel,
a quarter of a millisecond to milliseconds. The pass over textures picked
by index makes hundreds of those a frame while the world streams in, and
every other recording thread that mirrored a slot of the same heap stood
waiting for the lock. The sampling profiler, in a cutscene's first
seconds on an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (25 November): 450 ms a frame of the
recording threads waiting in HostHeap::mirror, 12 of 38 s of the pass in
host_texture_as.

For a slot made for a draw that is not made from this view yet, the
texture's host copy (or the placed texture's resource and its host copy)
is made first, with the lock not held; `make` then finds it. The view is
read from the title's slot before the lock, as it was right after it.

GPU: a placed texture found mapped is not asked about again page by page

After the pass over textures picked by index stages a texture, it asked
whether all of the texture's memory is there (texture::staged): a look
at the working set for every page, and a one-byte read through the
kernel for every page the process has not touched, which is every page
of a texture just streamed in. For a placed texture the pass had just
counted the mapped bytes block by block (mapped_bytes) and found all of
them. In a cutscene's first seconds on an RTX 4060 Laptop GPU the second
look was 8.4 of the pass's 38 s (the sampling profiler, 25 November),
on the recording thread that runs the pass.

A placed texture mapped_bytes found whole is taken as whole
(texture::staged_bytes gives its staged size without the look). Title
memory is mapped in 64 KiB pages, and a page mapped or unmapped later
makes the slot due again. Texture objects and partly mapped textures are
asked as before.

GPU: the write-watch journal is let go while the kernel is asked

`watch::writes` held the journal's lock for its GetWriteWatch call and
for the guards' walk when that failed. The copies a submission brings up
to date on several threads (VICTORY_WIDE_REFRESH=1) and the texture
refreshes each ask about their own range, and they stood in line for the
lock, one asking at a time: the sampling profiler on an RTX 4060 Laptop
GPU (25 November, normal play) found our submitting thread 48 ms a frame
waiting for it, of a 268 ms frame, and the wide workers on a processor 8 %
of the time.

The asking now runs with the lock let go, into a buffer of the thread's
own. Its range is noted busy in the journal meanwhile: a `writes` or
`asked` whose pages overlap it, and every asking ahead (`ask_ahead`,
`ask_once`), waits until its pages are in the journal, so nothing finds
pages reset by the kernel and not noted yet. Ranges that do not overlap
are asked at the same time. The pages found get their asking's number
when the lock is taken again; a number can only be later than before,
which copies a page again, never misses one.

With VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT=1, a present that found the present before it
still in a queue's line ran the old way: the title's thread ran the
queues' lines itself, holding the releaser's lock, while our submitting
thread stood waiting for that lock, and the next frame began with an
empty line. So only every other frame went behind: the frame log shows
pairs of a 3 ms and a 290 ms frame, and the sampling profiler (RTX 4060
Laptop GPU, 25 November) our thread 46 ms a frame waiting for the
releaser's lock and 27 ms with nothing to do.

The title's present now waits until our thread has shown the frame
before (one frame ahead at most, as before), then goes behind as well.
The wait is VICTORY_ASYNC_PRESENT_WAIT_MS (250 by default; 0: as
before); past it, a line that stands at a fence or memory value only the
title would meet runs the old way, which forces it. The 512-presents
line says how many waited in vain.

HLE: load a host DLL outside the module cache's lock

host::module held the module cache's lock while it called
LoadLibraryExA. Loading a DLL that is not loaded yet takes the OS
loader lock, and title code runs under that lock too (a title DLL's
thread attach, TLS callbacks run as threads start), where it can need
the cache: any first use of a host! function, or a late-bound title
DLL. One thread holding the cache and waiting for the loader lock,
another holding the loader lock and waiting for the cache: the process
hangs, and cannot even exit, as ExitProcess needs the loader lock too.

The cache is now looked up, then unlocked for the load, then locked
again to keep the handle; a thread that loaded the same DLL meanwhile
got the same module, which stays loaded.

gfx10: resolve the opcode name once, at decode time

`Instruction::name()` binary-searches the opcode table, and the pipeline
asks about every instruction eight times per translation: `ir::build`,
`structure`, `resource` (which has the most call sites), `io` and
`lower`. The answer cannot change - the encoding and opcode are decoded
from the words and never rewritten - so resolve it once when the
instruction is built and read the field after that.

Measured with the synthetic bench from #1002 (no game data), sixteen
interleaved rounds per arm, best of each, nanoseconds per instruction, at
256/1k/4k/16k instructions:

  resource     17 -> 9, 15 -> 7, 24 -> 16, 23 -> 15    (0.47-0.67)
  lower       511 -> 479, 428 -> 411, 440 -> 401, 477 -> 428  (0.90-0.96)
  io           27 -> 23, 26 -> 21, 26 -> 22, 30 -> 22   (0.73-0.85)
  whole       926 -> 881, 920 -> 874, 958 -> 921, 1019 -> 939 (0.92-0.96)

`decode` pays the one search it used to be spared (112 -> 115 at 16k,
inside the run-to-run spread); every stage after it reads a field. The
emitted DXIL is byte-identical at all four sizes.

XGameSave: a stray or unreadable version folder never costs the save

Recovery took any name `v<digits>` as a version, so a leftover `v01`
next to a committed `v1` parsed as version 1, and the cleanup rebuilt
the name as `v1` and deleted the committed save (#870). A correctly
named but unreadable newer entry (an empty `v2`, a file, a broken
manifest) did the same: `v1` was pruned as older, the read failed, and
the next update committed a fresh `v1` holding only the changed blobs,
which the following read pruned again.

Now only `v<N>` exactly as `commit` writes it is a version. `current`
takes the newest version whose manifest reads, removes only versions
below it, and leaves unreadable newer entries alone. An update goes
above the highest version name present, so a stray entry neither hides
the save nor blocks writes. With no readable version at all, reads and
updates still fail and nothing is removed.
